en: The Circumstances for Carving the Recorded Sayings of Xuefeng Twenty years ago, I dreamed of wandering through a desolate temple. There I saw the Patriarch Xuefeng seated upon it.

I immediately prostrated myself with my five limbs touching the ground. When the Master saw me, he smiled and, placing his hand upon my head, bestowed this prediction: "Revere and honor your teachers."
I revered him as I do my parents, yet my mind felt otherwise toward others. Last spring, the Great Layman Jisheng came to Min;
deeply grieving the decline of the ancestral temple, he exerted himself to restore it and invited Master Guhang to oversee the project.

At that time, I was accompanied by Shao Jiandun, and we followed him on foot with our staffs. Upon seeing the precious statue within the hall and the gatehouse and main halls, I was suddenly struck with a sense of wonder.
Like what is seen in a dream, because the master and disciple met, their connection endures even through the ages.

I am ashamed of my own drifting ignorance, yet I have received the teacher’s entrustment; the nourishing milk of the Dharma flows abundantly, its grace so profound it is difficult to repay. I often sigh at the shifting transformations of the world.

The traces of the teachings have gradually faded away; those wishing to seek the Master’s bequeathed words find but few remaining. From what survives amidst the ravages of woodworms, I have managed to recover but one or two fragments.
It happened that the venerable Zhiti visited me at my thatched cottage beyond the dust of the world and presented me with a volume for my inspection.
He felt great joy; he burned incense, washed his hands, and read it, unable to let go of the manuscript. However, he lamented that there were many misplaced folios (*kṣepaka*).
He returned home and brought it to Song’an, where he and the two practitioners Qinglin and Caoyuan searched for old editions and meticulously collated them.

It was only after a month that the work was completed. Just as they finished, Master Shiyu arrived at Xichan Monastery with his staff; as soon as they faced one another, [the author] immediately inquired about this record.
"Why have you not carved it? I replied, "I have specifically entrusted this to the engraver on this very day.

"How marvelous! the Master exclaimed. Without realizing it, we looked at one another and laughed. I then reflected that while the Master spoke these words seven hundred years ago, I am carving them seven hundred years later.
Within the palace of lapis lazuli, we walk hand in hand; there is nowhere that is not our own body, and no time when we are not together.

He said, "The Master is still here. To say that one must wait until the stone egg has completely peeled away and the tamarisk branches have fallen back down before he can come again is merely to join me in speaking of a dream."
In the summer of the Jīmōu year of the Chóngzhēn era, the layman Lín Hóngyǎn of Míngzhōng respectfully inscribed this preface to the *Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xuěfēng* while burning incense.
Among the remaining words of ancient patriarchs, those like Xuěfēng are truly difficult to find; yet, among them, it is Zhaozhou’s "I do not agree" that stands out.

This matter remains a point of doubt that continues to deceive and kill people to this day. Were it not for one who turns about within this very place and possesses the single eye, it would not be easy to expect even a lingering sap from a withered worm.
When the Layman of the Mountain Forest recounted his karmic conditions for entering the Way, he recorded the name "Xuefeng" in his dream;
our late master Yunmen marveled at this, as if Shide and Hanshan were simultaneously speaking of a dream.
The lay practitioner, through the extraordinary circumstances of his dream-body, could not bear to forget the Dharma lineage of Xuefeng.

He diligently searched through various manuscripts and obtained the draft of Xuansha, requesting that my late teacher provide a preface. Yet, he still harbored regret that the teachings of Xuefeng had not yet been fully disseminated.

By chance, while gathering among the clouds and waters, I discovered the complete collection; rejoicing at such an unprecedented find, I committed it to the carving blocks. This is precisely as the Mountain Hermit [Shan-yeh] arrived.
It was a day at Xichan Monastery. I happened to inquire about the *Recorded Sayings* (Yulu) of Xuefeng. The layman [the donor] responded with a leap of joy, saying, "How can its wonders be so great?
He then recounted the previous conversation in detail, along with the scenes from his dream, requesting a preface from me.

I humbly consider that when the layman dreamed of entering Xuefeng’s realm, what he saw was truly a purple-robed Arhat; for when he visited in person, the features were solemn and the robes were resplendent.
The "Golden Color" [case] where the robe was offered to the masterless monk—though it is recorded as such, one cannot avoid the doubt that arises when facing it directly.
Although this is an existing ancient woodblock, for those who seek a fresh perspective before their eyes, they must yet speak another word of realization;
only then might they truly meet Xuefeng face-to-face. As for what I personally cherish—the original dream of my late teacher from years past—it remains so today.
The dream was shattered in the mountains and wilds.
On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment in the year Wuyin (1638), the orthodox lineage of Caodong was transmitted.

I once saw a book titled *Candeng Shipu* (Genealogy of the Lamp of Chan), which refused to allow Longtan to be the successor of Tianhuang and instead insisted on arbitrarily making him the successor of Tianwang.
Furthermore, there was no such person as "Tianwang" (Heaven-King) to be found; thus, they had simply added a "Tianwang" to the lineage under Mazu.
He taught the descendants of Longtan to become Deshan and Xuefeng.
Having mastered the two traditions of Yunmen and Fayan, he took leave of the path of Shitou and moved his ancestral grave to that of Mazu.
Such demonic deeds he carried out openly without hesitation, yet ultimately there is no other evidence to verify them; it is merely based on the *Wudeng Huiyuan*.

The Imperial Decree relies solely on two spurious inscriptions cited in the *Xiàozhù* (Sub-commentary) as its evidence. How grievous! I intended to compose a rebuttal to rectify this, but lacked the leisure;
however, upon receiving the arguments presented by my Dharma brother, I read them through carefully.

My lifelong aspirations have been fulfilled, for it seems the spirits of the two schools have truly relied upon this to lend their prestige to a renowned pen, wielding the axe of Xiao to execute the demons. Thus, I compose this [work].
The words of Donggu, the chronicler of that monastic history, state: "His merit is not inferior to that of Yu. This refers precisely to this case.
According to the *Recorded Sayings of Xuefeng*, he himself claimed that he had transmitted this secret dharma-gate from the time of the former masters Deshan and Shitou onwards.
Furthermore, Qinshan asked: "Tianhuang spoke thus; Longtan also spoke thus.
These two elders were both fifth-generation descendants of Qingyuan; how could they have failed to record their own ancestors from afar?
Yet one traces Deshan back to Shitou, while the other affiliates Longtan with Tianhuang. This also reveals the true nature of our own kin."
To recount one’s own family genealogy is something that cannot be remotely usurped or interfered with by the oral reports of mere strangers;
this is self-evident. Furthermore, the *Preface to the Extensive Collection of Essential Teachings of Mount Gu* contained in the *Recorded Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters* states:
"Since the blossoming of the flower in the Shaoshi [Cave] that produced six petals, and the spreading of the lineage of Caoxi to all quarters, there emerged Shitou, who was styled 'The Pure'."
The *Jinpù* (Golden Shop) [commentary] states: "Because its standard is lofty and its diction archaic, its language is perilous and its principles profound.

Consequently, for generations of descendants, whether their steps were wide or narrow, they did not differ by so much as a hair’s breadth. It further records that the late Master Xingxing, a Dharma heir of Xuefeng—who himself was the fifth generation descendant of Shitou—wrote in the postscript to the *Guǎngjí*:
"Gushan Yan received the Dharma from Xuefeng Cun; he was thus in the direct line of Shitou."
Sixth Patriarch said: "Based on this, is this not yet another genealogy of the Stonehead (Shitou) lineage? For instance, Mingjiao Yongshou was the fourth-generation descendant of Yunmen;

he was ten generations removed from Stonehead. Although the lineal succession is somewhat distant, those who praised him called him 'the one and only person south of the Northern Dipper' among the eminent monks of the Song dynasty.
He authored the *Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma* (*Chuanfa Zhengzong Ji*), exerting great effort..."
He corrected the errors in the *Fu fazang zhuan* (The Transmission of the Dharma-treasury). Among these, he produced clear textual evidence from the great sūtras and śāstras.

When Emperor Renzong read this, he marveled incessantly at how [the Master] practiced the Way for its own sake rather than for fame, and served the Dharma for its own sake rather than for his own person.

Consequently, the great figures of the time, such as Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu, all unanimously turned toward him. Thus, by means of this, the orthodox lineage was established, and by this, the patriarchal succession was definitively settled.
According to their records up to the present day: did not the successor of Shitou go by the name of Tianhuang Daowu of Jingzhou?
And did not the successor of Tianhuang go by the name of Longtan Chongxin of Lishui?

Given his profound, vast, and great wisdom, he was precisely the one who, five hundred years ago, cleared the false accusations against Bodhidharma; how could he possibly fail to recognize his own tenth-generation ancestor?
To acknowledge this and yet trouble later generations of philologists to point out the way for them— dragging them by the bridle to seek their father’s chin—
is to see much of their own lack of discernment. What is even more lamentably ridiculous is that while ancient scholars cited such texts as mere footnotes,
still preserving the principle of "suspending judgment where doubt exists," the present day instead blindly trusts forged inscriptions and arbitrarily alters the Dragon Canon.
How dare you be so audacious and unrestrained as to reach such heights! I am filled with indignation; having been provoked by your bold rhetoric, I could not help but draw my sword to assist you.
As for what you say—that you act for the sake of the Way and not for fame, and for the sake of the Dharma and not for yourself—[this is merely empty talk].
This is also our own concern today; it cannot be left to others. On this day at Hengshan, we are not far from one another in terms of hearing and sight.
I do not know how my Dharma brother’s recent condition is. Yet, there has been news of his voice reaching us, so that the ancestral style has not perished.
Furthermore, he sent his robe and alms bowl as a token of faith. Even up to the Fifth Patriarch, there was still a distinction between the primary and the secondary. This too—
It was for the sake of the robe and bowl. Once the Sixth Patriarch’s Dharma path had spread widely, the robe and bowl were no longer necessary;

I feared only that people might use the side and the orthodox lineages as a pretext for contention. Recently, there have been those who, being strange and deluded, do not understand this meaning and instead create much more dispute and error.
Therefore, in my writings as a lay practitioner, I could not help but take the words of the Great Master Xuefeng as my guiding pointer.

Furthermore, within this work, I have dissected and explained everything without omission. When I carved the *Xuefeng Lu* (Record of Xuefeng), I was especially apprehensive that future generations might lack a reliable source for their studies.
Because [this record] is confused by its eccentricities and anomalies, I have specifically set forth the words of the layman Yu to represent it.

Compiled by the Layman Shanshu of Min, Lin Hongyan: The Master’s name was Yicun.
He was a son of the Zeng family from Nanan County, Quanzhou. His family lineage had long been devoted to Buddhism; since his birth, the Master abhorred the consumption of meat and pungent vegetables.
While still in his swaddling clothes, whenever he heard the sounds of bells and chanting, or saw banners, flowers, or sacred images, he would invariably move with deep emotion.
At the age of twelve, while traveling with his father to Yujian Temple in Putian, he encountered the Vinaya Master Qingxuan and immediately prostrated himself, saying:

"I am your teacher," [the master said]. He then remained to serve him. At seventeen, he shaved his head and visited the Great Master Hongzhao of Fuyong. Hongzhao stroked his head and regarded him as a vessel of great potential.
Later, he went to Baocha Temple in Youzhou to receive the full precepts. After participating in various Chan assemblies for a long time, his karmic affinity was realized with Deshan.
During the Xian Tong era of the Tang dynasty, he returned to Mount Xuefeng in Min to establish a monastery, where his disciples gathered in great numbers.
Emperor Yizong conferred upon him the title Chan Master Zhenjue and bestowed a purple *kāṣāya*. While the Master was serving as the head cook at Dongshan, as he was washing rice, Dongshan asked:
Rinsing the sand to remove the rice; rinsing the rice to remove the sand. The Master said, "Sand and rice are removed all at once.
Shanshan asked, "What will the assembly eat? The Master then turned the rice basin upside down. Shanshan said, "According to these conditions, this should belong to Deshan.
One day, Dongshan asked the Master, "What have you been doing? The Master replied, "I have been making a trough. Dongshan asked, "How many blows from the axe did it take to finish it?"
The Master said, "It was formed by a single stroke of the axe. Mount Shandao said, "That is still a matter of this side. What about the matter of that side?
The Master said, "It is such that there is no place to apply the hand. Mount Shandao said, "That is still a matter of this side. What about the matter of that side?"
The Master retired. While the Master was steaming rice, Dongshan asked, "How much did you steam today? The Master said, "Two *shí*. Dongshan said, "Is it not enough?
The Master said, "There are some among them who do not eat. Dongshan said, "What if they all eat? The Master had no reply. (Xian Yunju spoke on his behalf:
"If they all eat, then one does not see that there is anything insufficient. When Dongshan saw the Master coming, he said, "Enter."

Tou said, "I thought you would one day atop a solitary peak, having built a thatched hut, propagate the Great Teaching—and yet you still speak such words.
The Master replied, "Truly, I am not yet settled. Tou said, "If it is truly so for you, then according to what you..."
"Wherever you see [a point of] attachment, it will come to you one by one. In those instances, I shall provide you with proof; in those that are not, I shall eradicate them for you.

Baizhang said, 'From now until thirty years hence, you must strictly avoid mentioning it. Furthermore, I saw Dongshan’s verse on crossing the water, which says: 'Strictly avoid following others...'"
"Seeking," he said, "is to be far removed from me. 'He is now truly I; I am now not he.

Later, after [the Master] had taken up residence there, a monk asked, "What did you gain upon meeting Deshan that you then retired? The Master replied, "I went empty-handed and returned empty-handed. There were two [versions].
A monk approached. The Master pushed open the gate of his hut with his hand, stepped out, and said, "What is this?

The monk also said, "What is this? The Master lowered his head and returned to the hut. As the monk was taking his leave, the Master asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "To Hunan. The Master said:
I have a fellow practitioner living at Yantou; I am sending a letter to him for you. The letter says: "Your disciple [Name] writes to his senior brother:
Since I attained the Way at Mount Ao, until this very day, I have remained full and never hungry. Your fellow practitioner [Name] writes."
The monk arrived at Yantou and was asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from Xuefeng; I have a letter for the Master.
Yantou received it and then asked the monk, "What other words or phrases did he say? The monk then recounted the previous conversation. Yantou said, "What did he say?"
The monk said nothing and bowed his head as he returned to his hut. Baizhang said, "Alas! In the beginning, I regretted not telling him the final word.
Had I told him, no one in the world could have stood against Old Xue. At the end of the summer retreat, the monk requested further instruction on the previous matter.
Baizhang said, "Why did you not ask sooner? The monk replied, "I did not dare to be casual about it. Baizhang said, "Although Xuefeng gave it to me..."

Upon ascending the hall, the assembly had stood for a long time. The Master said, "O sons of the patriarchs, what are you seeking by coming up here when the bell and drum are struck?"
What grievance is there? Do you still know shame? What fault is there? Looking at you all, there are few who possess true penetration.
My situation is unavoidable; what I have told you—what is it? As soon as you enter the gate, I deliberate with you, yet you immediately accept it as such.
It would be better to save your mental energy; do not let it go to waste until you reach old age.
"It comes from the Master’s own mouth. Do you understand? After a long silence, he spoke again: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot chant it;
the twelve divisions of the teachings cannot record it. How could those who nowadays merely chew on phlegm and spittle ever understand it? I have always told you this."
What is it? Come closer and seek a place to receive an answer. Will you recognize it even after as many donkey-years as there are?

Having no other recourse, I speak to you in this way; I have already deceived you flatly. When I told you that before you had even entered the gate, we had already reached a mutual understanding, did you understand?
This too is the "old woman’s heart" (compassionate persistence); you simply refuse to acknowledge the point where effort is exhausted.
You should take this upon yourself. You merely know how to step forward, seeking words and seeking phrases.

I tell you that the entire universe is this gate of liberation, yet you refuse to enter it altogether. You only know how to run about aimlessly within it; whenever you meet someone, you ask, "Which one is me? Are you not ashamed?
It is only you who bring this humiliation upon yourself. This is why countless people die of thirst by the river, even while there is rice to eat.
People suffering hunger within the winnowing baskets are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Do not treat this with indifference, O son of the Elder (Upādhyāya).
If you have truly not yet attained awakening, you must certainly awaken before it is too late; do not let your time pass in vain.

Do not merely associate with others to engage in empty chatter and deceptive talk that misleads people—this is a matter concerning each person’s own lot. You must also apply yourself with vigor and care. Bodhidharma...

The Way has been passed down through polishing; I have transmitted mind-to-mind without establishing written words. But what, pray tell, is the mind of these people? Since it cannot be categorized, let it rest.
If you have not clarified this matter of your own self, where will you find a place to dissolve all these manifold delusions?

In the midst of time, there is no place for you to settle yourself; thus, you perceive distinctions between the ordinary and the holy, between male and female, and between monastics and laypeople. High...

There is a distinction between the low and the superior. Before the Great Earth, they are like those clamoring while spreading sand. Not for a single thought-moment have they ever turned back toward the divine light;
they wander through birth and death, never ceasing throughout kalpas. One must feel great shame and remorse; each of you must exert yourselves!
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "The initial mind and the subsequent mind do not understand; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "What should I instruct you?
The monk pressed further, "How can it be that I do not understand? The Master said, "It is you who do not understand; I am without fault. The monk pressed further.

[The student] again requested instruction. The Master said, “Do you understand? [The student] stepped forward and said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “Alas! Alas! How can it be so difficult to save you?

[The student] asked, “What are the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional? The Master said, “Setting aside the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional for a moment, as for your own matter—how is it?
[The student] stepped forward and said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “If you do not even understand your own self, how can you understand the two truths?”
Question: What are the two truths and the three truths? Question: What are the Buddhas? The Master said: "Do not touch upon what is taboo. The questioner pressed further:
"What is not touching upon what is taboo? The Master said: "To understand shamelessness. Question: This student has recently entered the monastic community;
I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said: "I would rather have my body shattered into fine dust than ever blind a monk."
Yunmen said, "All you venerable sons of the Buddha, why have you come here?
Is there anything lacking within your own sphere of being? Not even a single blade of grass has ever been able to cover it.
Why then do you not understand? You intend to step forward and seek it, desiring only for others to speak of it. Even for kalpas, you would never dare."
To be thus mutually entangled is your own personal affair; why do you not understand how to leave it?

You only ever manage to grasp the affairs within others' houses, merely consuming the spittle of your teachers from the sidelines and forming intellectual interpretations within the realm of consciousness.
Suddenly, when questioned about the affairs within your own house, you resort to mere superficial words. When confronted by one with clear eyes...
Suddenly struck down, one cannot go on; it is a vast, dark expanse, like a lacquer bucket. This is simply because in your past travels you did not meet extraordinary people.
Therefore it is said: "The grievance lies in the beginning. From the outset, matters cannot be as they seem. Why do you speak in such a manner?
You sons of the Buddha, matters from kalpas as numerous as dust motes exist only in this very moment. If you attempt to shift them even by a thread...
To have one's hair on the ground is to be a man who has lost his life. If you merely uphold a single word, you will remain a wild fox spirit for kalpas.
If you are truly sharp and quick-witted, you need not wait for a teacher to open the mouth of a frog. Do you understand?
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, “The single path of Caoxi is known throughout the land; what, then, was Xuefeng’s intent?
The Master said, “Under the gate of a physician, there are many ghosts of illness. A monk asked, “What further words have been transmitted from ancient times to the present?

The Master said, “Look for yourself. The monk stepped forward and said, “Is it that you have no sight or hearing? The Master said, “One must not suffer from deafness. A monk asked, “...? [The text ends here.]
[Question: "When the way of sovereign and subject is in harmony, what then? The Master said: "I have never acquired the household goods of the Old Barbarian. [Question:
"Without offending against the immediate occasion, please speak, Master. The Master said: "Look at you; you lack the capacity for self-determination. [Question:
"Is there still a place here where one can find a phrase? The Master said: "Shut those two pieces of skin. [Question: "Without relying on the three [vehicles]..."

[The monk] asked, "How is it when there is not even an inch [of cloth]? The Master said, "You are a man of transgression. [Another] asked, "When one beyond the secular world wears not even an inch of silk, how is it?
The Master said, "How could it be so? [The monk] further asked, "Is there no teacher of knowledge appearing in the world?"
The Master said, "Drag him out! A questioner asked, "When one has reached the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, how does one take the next step?
The Master said, "To stir is to perish. A questioner asked, "If one uses a bowstring as a bridge, what happens when one crosses it? The Master said, "One will fall into a pit."
Question: "What is it like when biting a spinning wheel? The Master said: "It passes through the cheeks. Question: "How can one draw near to that which is most supreme and most noble?
The Master said: "Even a person of no affairs cannot draw near to it. The questioner pressed further: "What of one who has attained the state of being bodiless?"
"Is it possible to approach and draw near? The Master said, "It is not an obstacle; you may approach according to your capacity. The monk asked further, "Once one has approached, what then?
The Master said, "The hornet does not cling to its old nest. The Master then said, "All of you come here saying, 'I am drawing near.
But how do you draw near? If you intend to draw near, you are already distant; if you intend to approach, you are already far away. A monk hesitated.

Question: The Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk and said, "Do you understand? Question: "What is it like when one does not dwell alongside a single thing? The Master said, "It deafens your ears. Question:
"If one does not spare one's mouth, is it permitted to engage in discussion? The Master said, "One who is not startled by imminent peril.
The Master further said, "The Buddhas of the three periods of time are but men from within the grass; the ten sutras and five treatises are but shackles."
Donkey stake. The eighty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is merely the head of a grass hut used for bolting food and talking.
The twelve divisions of the teaching are matters from the mouth of a frog. Do you understand? Therefore it is said:

"If among the thousands and hundreds of people today there were even one person who thoroughly and greatly agreed with me to act as a donkey to carry my things—what fault would there be in making offerings to such a one?"
Question: "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different? The Master said: "Venerable, for what purpose do you travel on pilgrimage? Question:
"As for the one path leading upward, I do not yet understand how it is. The Master said: "You would have your mouth locked. He further said:
"The Buddhas of the three periods cannot emerge from within this; not a single word can be added to the Great Canon of the Teachings; nor can the teachers of the world [penetrate it]."
"Facing this way, everything is reduced to a hundred fragments. Do you understand? If you people can truly attain clarity, you will avoid being deluded by others;

even when there are words and phrases, you will have no further doubts. If you yourself have not yet attained clarity, you must by all means refrain from making empty claims, lest you waste your time in vain.
Do not merely memorize a word or two under the chins of teachers from various quarters."
To take these phrases and apply them to one's own breast is a great error, brothers. I say that it is merely these three inches that can kill a person and can bring a person to life.
Ordinarily, when I ask monks, "What is it? they immediately begin to babble on, their mouths flapping incessantly.
As for those like this, when will they ever be able to take responsibility? Let me ask you, you sons of the patriarchs:
do the elders of various quarters speak of matters to you, Dharma-heirs? Have they ever given you instruction? Have they ever discussed the Way of Chan with you?
You must examine this thoroughly and investigate it with great care. Question: What is the matter of face-to-face encounter?
The Master said, "A thousand li is not far. A questioner asked, "What is the matter here? The Master said, "What is it? The questioner pressed further, "I beg the Master for instruction.
The Master said, "He has already gone to the kingdom of Silla. The Master offered this saying: "Countless people die of thirst by the river;
those who suffer hunger beside the grain basket are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—not merely one or half a person."
Brothers, if your faculties and thoughts are slow and hesitant, you must diligently remain grounded.
Do not merely spend the winter on this side and the summer on that side, gathering up a few drops of mucus and spittle and claiming that the affairs of a lifetime are finished.

To merely intend to transcribe and record [the teachings] is entirely the reliance upon intellectual learning and conceptual understanding. Such as these, I call them "guests beneath the frog’s robe. I also call them...
[The Master] said, "A black ox lies dead in the water; do you understand? A question was asked: "When the six states present treasures, does the King accept them?
The Master said, "The family style of the Old Barbarian is not like that of a roadside inn. A question was asked: "What is the family style of the Master?
The Master said, "In the entire world, there is no one so deluded as this. A question was asked: "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same?"
"This is a distinction. The Master said, "The sound of thunder shakes the earth, yet it is not heard within the room.
Question: "What is the mark of a great man? The Master said, "There is a share for those who gaze up in reverence. Question: "As soon as there are words and phrases, they are all errors.

I wonder, what is the matter that is not in error? The Master said, "Where would your eyes go? Question: "When Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī conversed, what was it? The Master said, "It was like two mirrors reflecting each other."
[The student] asked about a matter. The Master said, “Your meaning has fallen into error. [The student] asked, “The sea of suffering has no boat; how can one cross it?

The Master said, “Not even an inch of grass is borrowed. [The student] asked, “After one single push, what then? The Master said, “Hearing the sound of the pear tree, you must strictly avoid cultivation or construction upon your life.
[The student] asked, “What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, “It is like talking in one’s sleep under a clear blue sky and bright sun—what is there to do?”
Question: Why does the rotten wood not stop before the waterfall and the cliff? The Master said: "It is urgent. Question: When many hands sift for gold, who is the one that obtains it?
The Master said: "The worthy one does not obtain it. The questioner followed up: "When the clear stream is exhausted, where does the gold go?
The Master said: "When the water arrives, the channel is formed. Question: What is it like when there is stillness and no dependence? The Master said: "It is still [a state]."
[The Master] was ill. [A monk] asked, "What is it like after turning back? The Master said, "The boatman has gone down to Yangzhou.
A monk asked, "Dongshan and Daowu often applied themselves to this point. I do not know what its meaning is. The Master said, "I have been up to Dongshan nine times.
As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "Drag that monk out! A monk asked, "An ancient said, 'The Master then fell. The Master immediately fell over.
He lay down. After a long while, he rose and said, "What were you asking just now? The monk asked again.
The Master replied, "A man who lives in vain and dies in vain. Question: "Before the patterns have yet been distinguished, is there still a master? The Master said:
"If there is a master, it is immediately the literary pattern. The student asked, "Does it then turn back? The Master said, "Look for yourself. Question:
"What is it like when the tip of the arrow is exposed? The Master said, "A skilled hand does not hit the mark. The student asked, "What is it like when the eye is completely devoid of a target?
The Master said, "It does no harm; you are a skilled hand in your own right. Question: "What is the matter beneath the patched robe?"
The Master said, "Seek it beneath the patched robe. A monk asked, "I have heard the Master say that this monk has come here carrying a skeleton from Dingzhou.
I do not know what object he is carrying. The Master said, "I have told you clearly.
The monk asked, "Is there still a stake driven into empty space? The Master said, "I say that empty space itself is the stake. The monk... [remained silent].
He took his leave of the Master and said, "I have suddenly arrived at another place.
An elder asked, "What instructions did the Master give you to point the way for others? How would you express them? The Master asked, "Do you understand my words? He replied, "I do not."
The Master said, "For now, let us make a lacquered bucket.
He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying, "As for this water buffalo, how many years old is it? The assembly remained silent.
The Master said, "It is seventy-nine. A monk asked, "Why does the Master act as a water buffalo? The Master replied, "What fault is there in that?"
Question: "What kind of person are you, Preceptor? The Master said: "I am a layman. The questioner pressed: "Why then do you enter the Sangha hall?
The Master said: "What offense is there in that? Question: "An ancient said: 'When meeting a man who has attained the Way on the road, do not respond with speech or silence.
I wonder, what should one use to respond? The Master said: "Just drink some tea and go. Question: "I have heard from the Preceptor..."
There was still something further to say. "The Three Vehicles' teachings are transmitted outside [of them]. What is this matter of the 'separate transmission'?
The Master said, "Why do you not fear that the monks will laugh at you? A questioner asked, "What is it like when there is nothing at all to think about?

The Master said, "Why are you sitting again within the realm of the aggregates (*skandhas*)? The questioner pressed, "What then happens afterwards? The Master said, "Why do you keep trying to pass through it?"
A monk asked, "I have only just reached the point where I cannot distinguish what is before me; I beg the Master to break through it for me. The Master said, "Who would break open your pile of dung?
The monk prepared to offer a reply, but the Master shouted him out. The Master asked another monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, [as the text ends].
"Divine Light has arrived," [a monk] said. The Master said, "By day it is called sunlight; by night it is called firelight. What is Divine Light? The monk had no reply.
The Master spoke on his behalf: "Sunlight. Firelight. A monk asked, "The twelve divisions of the teachings are expounded for the sake of ordinary people.
What is the matter that is not expounded for the sake of ordinary people? The Master said, "It does not require more than a single verse of 'Willow Branches' (Yangliuzhi)."
Question: An ancient said, "One must know the matter that lies beyond the Buddha; only then does one have a share in the discourse.
What is this discourse? The Master said: "What do you say? Question: When a monk comes in such a manner, how do you, Reverend, deliberate with him?
The Master said: "What do you say? Question: What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said: "O Benevolent One."
"What is the meaning of 'this' right now? [The student] asked, "What is the one sword? The Master said, "A dead man. [The student] pressed further, "Not dead?
The Master said, "His head has been falling for a long time. [The student] asked, "What is the whole ball? The Master said, "How can you deal with it?
[The student] asked, "What was the intent behind the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant? The Master took up his staff and drove him out.
Question: Having shaved one's hair, donned the dyed robes, and received the Buddha’s protection as a disciple, why is it not permitted to acknowledge the Buddha?
The Master said: "A good thing is not as good as having none at all. Question: What is the matter of face-to-face encounter? The Master said: "What is this? Question:
Those who come from afar do so because they do not understand this very thing. What is this thing? The Master said: "Do you understand? The questioner pressed on: "How about that?"
"How can this be demonstrated to others? The Master said, "This fellow runs about in confusion; what is he fit for conversation with? A monk asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "Under the Dharma-forest, there is no throne for a Son of Heaven. A monk asked, "I do not ask about the events of the forty-nine years;
how was it before those forty-nine years? The Master said, "You shrimp-mouthed fellow, what are you disputing?"

"What a pity! The monk prepared to offer a word in response, but the Master gave a shout and sent him out. A monk asked, "When one urgently seeks to find a point of connection, what is it like when the response is swift?
The Master said, "What are you saying? The monk hesitated, and the Master called for the Rector. When the Rector responded, the Master said:
“Go on general labor duty. A monk asked, “Who is the master of Xuefeng? The Master said, “You ignorant fellow who cannot distinguish good from evil!
He then dragged him out. A monk asked, “What is the path that leads upward? The Master said, “Thank you for pointing it out. A monk asked, “What is the matter beyond the Buddha?
The Master sang the *Langtao Sha* (Riversand Washed Away). A monk asked, “When the Master went to Tiantai, did you see Zhiyi?”

[The monk] said, "None. The Master said, "Today you have emerged from the head, yet you have encountered a dozing old man. [The monk] asked, "I am in urgent need of a point of entry; I pray the Master will give me instruction.
The Master said, "Suffering! Suffering! [The monk] asked, "I ask directly; I pray the Master will speak. The Master said, "Excellent."
Question: "The sea is vast and the clouds are deep; how can one cross it? The Master said, "I shall lend you a favorable wind.
The student continued, "Set up the boat and oars, and please ferry me across. The Master said, "This sleepyhead! You will not even know when you have reached the shore.
Question: "What is the most intimate place? The Master struck him in the mouth with his staff. Question: "What is it like when there is neither question nor answer?"
The Master said, "Dull-witted fellow. A monk asked, "What about when one comes with a face struck by a blow? The Master said, "Say what?
As the monk prepared to speak further, the Master said, "You have asked in vain. A monk asked, "What about when one has swallowed up Vairocana?
The Master said, "Have you returned safely from Fuchou? When the monk asked again, the Master simply rose and left. A monk asked, "What about when there is no transgression?"
A monk asked, "What about the 'Jie'? The Master shouted and sent him out. A monk asked, "What is the song of the cowherd boy?
The Master then performed a dance and went out of the Dharma Hall. A monk asked, "What is the matter before one's eyes? The Master said, "What is it?
A monk asked, "What is that which lies beyond words? The Master said, "Ask! Ask! When the monk asked again, the Master said, "Drag him out! A monk asked, "The ancients..."
"When face-to-face presentation occurs, how is it? The Master replied, "It is. He pressed further, "What is this face-to-face presentation?
The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven! A monk asked, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?
The Master said, "How do you handle your own affairs? He pressed further, "What is that? The Master said, "No-self. Then he asked the monk, "And you? What about you? The monk had no reply.
The Master said, "I recognize you. [The monk] asked, "All words and phrases, as well as all points of attainment, are entirely subsumed within the summit of the great chiliocosm.
I wonder, what is it like beyond that summit? The Master said, "Ask! Ask! The monk asked again. The Master said, "You lacquer bucket!"
[The Master] went out. A question was asked: "What is the reality that meets the eye? The Master said: "Heaven! Heaven! A question was asked:
"Apart from words and phrases, who is Xuefeng? The Master said: "On this great earth, there has never been such a muddled fellow."
Question: "In all directions, people are teaching according to their own capacity. I wonder, Master, how is it here?

The Master said: "What have I told you? The questioner pressed further: "It is not right not to receive people. The Master said: "What is there to converse with? Question: [The questioner asked again.]
"My eyes were originally correct; when did they become distorted because of the teacher? The Master said, "Meeting Bodhidharma while lost. The student asked, "Where are my eyes now?
The Master said, "Obtained them, but not from the teacher. Question: "When the 'blow-off-hair' sword is used, is it still held in the hand?
The Master said, "Three inches have fallen to the ground; do you know it yet? Question: "What is it like when the precious sword hangs in the air?"
The Master said, "This headless fellow. A question was asked: "What is the matter of the separate transmission outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles?

The Master said, "You must also know the proper time. A question was asked: "At the point where a student cannot speak it, I ask the Master to speak for us. The Master said, "I cherish people for the sake of the Dharma.
A question was asked: "When one is close to encountering [the truth], how is it? The Master said, "Do not touch upon what is taboo. A question was asked.
"What is the Dharma-body? The Master said, "Though it be a mouth born of conditions, one must not bite on a piece of excrement.
A monk asked, "If I ask, it brings trouble upon my ancestors; if I do not ask, what then? The Master said, "I shall sing forth the matter of the ancestors.

The monk pressed further, "The student is unable to grasp it; I beg you once more for instruction. The Master said, "I knew well that you would not distinguish between good and evil. [The monk] asked, "As for such as..."
"What is this matter of transcending the world? The Master said, "Though you are a junior, it shall not defile you.
The student asked further, "What is it like when one has transcended the world and when one has not? The Master said, "Why are you so impolite? The Master spoke again.
There was once a man wrestling. Having thrown down his opponent with the first punch, he raised his head. At that moment, a monk came forward and said, "Come out!
Master, what kind of trickery is this? The Master said, "You have fallen over. A questioner asked, "When one grows up and remains silent, on what do the multitude rely?
The Master said, "Just save yourself. A questioner asked, "If you intend to act, it becomes a defilement; how is it when you do not act in such a way? The Master said, "..."
"You must take it up yourself. The student asked, "I do not yet understand where one who is learning should take it up.

The Master said, "It is still being cast away. The student asked, "If one recognizes this very thing, how is that? The Master said, "Hush! A question was asked: "To grasp it is to fall into existence;
not to grasp it is to fall into non-existence. Apart from these two paths, please, Master, speak. The Master said, "When the weather is clear and dry, you are unwilling to go."
"Simply let it rain on your head. A monk asked, "I have heard the Master say that the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot show their heads here.
I do not understand what fault the Buddhas have such that they cannot show their heads.
The Master said, "You shameless fellow! A monk asked, "I do not ask about the second blow; what is the first blow? The Master said, "You..."
"Can it be placed in victory? [The monk] asked, "What is the student’s own-eye? The Master said, "Planting flowers upon a stone.
The Master then asked the monk, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Be careful.
[The monk] asked, "Where has the Great Master Xiyuan gone after his passing? The Master said, "Not only you, but all the people in the entire world do not know either."
Question: “What is profound study? The Master said: “What more would you seek? The Master asked a monk:
“Where have you come from? The monk replied: “From Mount Gui. The Master said: “What words or phrases did Mount Gui have? The monk replied:
“I once asked him, ‘What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? and Mount Gui sat in silence. The Master said: “Do you approve of him? The monk said: [“Yes.”]
The other would not consent. The Master said, "Tishan is an ancient Buddha; you must go quickly and repent.
One day, while the Master was burning fire inside the Sangha hall, he closed both the front and back doors and cried out, "Save the fire! Save the fire! The Master did not open the door.
Xuansha took a piece of firewood and threw it in through the window; the Master then opened the door.
Ascending the hall, the assembly gathered. A monk bowed respectfully and departed. The Master said, "If everyone were like this monk, how much mental effort would I save!
Xuansha said, "Master, by receiving people in such a manner, you are blinding the eyes of the entire city of Min.
The Master asked, "What do you say? Xuansha said, "A good thirty blows for you! The Master then offered this statement: "Throughout the great..."
"The earth is the single eye of a śramaṇa. Where will you all go to defecate?
A monk arrived at Zhaozhou, and Zhaozhou asked, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "I have come from Xuefeng. Zhaozhou asked, "What sayings or phrases has Xuefeng been teaching lately?
The monk related the previous conversation. Zhaozhou said, "When you leave here, take a spade with you. Later, Xuedou commented on this.
[The Master] said: "This monk did not come from Xuefeng. What a pity for Zhaozhou’s spade! Master Lingguan used to sit alone with his door closed.
One day, the Master went to knock on the door. As soon as Lingguan opened it, the Master grabbed him and asked, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage?
Lingguan spat at him and said, "Wild fox spirit! He pushed him away and closed the door again. The Master said, "He simply wanted to be recognized."
The Old Man asked: "What is the student’s fundamental matter? The Master said: "The autumn night is so long;
why do you nod off during the day? He asked: "What is the extraordinary matter? The Master said: "Question! Question! Question!"
"How does a person who is utterly blind pass their days? The Master said, "By drinking tea and eating rice. The student asked, "Is it not a waste of one's days?
The Master said, "It is a waste of one's days. The student asked, "How can one avoid wasting one's days? The Master said, "What is it?"
Question: "What is 'different species'? The Master took up his staff and drove him out. Question:

"What is the single principle within the steps? The Master said, "What principle is there right now? Question: "When one comes charging face-first, what then? The Master said, "You have missed it. Question:
"Before patterns and colors were yet distinguished, what was it like? The Master gave him a blow. The student stepped forward and said, "The Master has gone too far!"
[The monk] said, "It is coarse. The Master said, "I do not know whether it is you who are coarse or I who am coarse. [The monk] asked, "What is the matter that meets the eye?
The Master raised his whisk. The monk stepped forward and said, "Is this not it? The Master said, "What is it? The monk had no reply. [The monk] asked, "How is it with the immediate matter?
The Master said, "I have never seen anyone ask such a thing. The monk stepped forward and said, [further questioning].
[The monk] immediately asked the Master, “What about now, O Reverend? The Master shouted, “You spiritless fellow! [The monk] asked, “What is the style of the ancients?
The Master said, “I have never encountered them. [The monk] pressed further, “Why has the Reverend never encountered them?
The Master said, “Where would you go to encounter the ancients? The monk was speechless. [The monk] asked, “What is the matter within [it]? The Master—
[The Master] said, "Go for now; we shall deliberate on this another time. A question was asked: "What is the matter beyond words?
The Master said, "What are you looking for here? The student stepped forward and said, "I am asking the Master right now. The Master said, "I thought you were a clever fellow."

"From the very beginning, you have been a bag of delusions. The student asked, "I do not dare ask much; I beg the Master for a single word on the essential point. The Master said, "Do not ask so much.
The student pressed further, "How can one avoid asking so much? The Master said, "Drag him out!"
Question: "What is the primordial originality? The Master said: "From where have you received this news? The monk replied:
"If there were any news, it would not be the primordial originality. The Master asked: "What, then, is the primordial originality?
The monk had no reply. The Master said: "Ask me, and I will tell you. The monk then asked. The Master took the monk’s patched robe and stripped it off.

[The Master] struck him several times with his staff and drove him out. A question was asked: "If one intends to separate by a thousand miles, I do not know how the process of polishing and refining proceeds.
The Master said, "It is already a thousand miles. A question was asked: "When the ancient barrier does not turn, what then? The Master said, "Even turning, it is not yet answered."
[The student] said, "It does not turn. The Master said, "Try turning it and see. [The student] asked, "I have heard the Master say, 'There is a thing that secretly aids people.
Yet, alas, people do not know it. How does it secretly aid people? The Master said, "How could you possibly know?

[The student] asked, "What is the Hall of the Empty King? The Master said, "Large and small. [The student] stepped forward and asked, "What is the Buddha of the Empty King? The Master said, "What is this?"
[The Master said: "Ma. A question was asked: "I have heard the Master say, 'Containing the Abbot’s Quarters. I do not know what it is that is contained. The Master said:
"Come out of the Abbot’s Quarters and I will discuss it with you. The questioner stepped forward and said: "Right now, where are you?
The Master said: "Have you come out yet? A question was asked: "When a student intends to return to his hometown, what then? The Master said: "Where are you right now?"

The Recorded Sayings of Great Master Xuefeng Zhijue, Volume II (Record of the Emperor’s Invitation to the Master and Xuansha to Enter the Inner Quarters to Discuss the Buddha-Mind Seal; Compiled by Miaode).
The Great King invited the Master and Xuansha to enter the inner quarters to discuss the Buddha-mind seal. The Great King questioned the two Chan masters.
"The Buddhas and the Dharma have transmitted the secret heart-seal; I beg the Master to explain it to me in its true essence.

Furthermore, since the time of the Patriarchs and Buddhas, what cause and effect must one ultimately cultivate to attain Buddhahood? The Master said, "One must see one's nature before one can attain Buddhahood.
The King asked, "What is meant by 'seeing one's nature'? The Master said, "It is seeing one's own original nature. The King asked, "Does it have form and shape?"

The Master said, "To see one's own original nature means there is nothing at all to be seen; this is a teaching difficult to believe. It is that which hundreds of thousands of Buddhas have equally attained.
The King asked, "Can it be attained? The Master said, "If one were to extol this matter, the entire world could not exhaustively describe it.
Yet if it was personally transmitted by Bodhidharma, it was but a single word, which immediately transforms the ordinary person into a sage—it is no small matter."
This matter: if one awakens to it, it is in a single instant; if one does not awaken to it, it spans kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Great King, within the Great Treasury of the Teachings, all the sutras and treatises—thousands upon ten thousands—are solely for the sake of this One Mind. From patriarch to patriarch, this One Mind has been transmitted.

However, as I, this mountain monk, explain this matter to Your Majesty, it must not be approached with haste. To point directly to the true nature: Great King, because of this matter, I, this mountain monk, [have come here].
Each has a following of several hundred or a thousand people, yet for twenty or thirty years they have all practiced this matter in secret;
not even one or two among them has been able to truly uphold it, let alone this Dharma-gate, which was transmitted from one person to another by the Buddhas of the past.

Furthermore, Your Majesty is a sagacious Son of Heaven, daily adjudicating the affairs of the mountains and rivers for the myriad people; if you harbor deluded thoughts, how could you possibly compete [with the truth]?
"I have encountered this true Dharma-gate. I pray that Your Majesty will serve as the sovereign of the Buddha-dharma and save and protect all living beings through the tip of your pen;
would this not be a most auspicious thing? Upon hearing this exhortation, the Great King felt redoubled joy.

He further asked the two masters, "I, the Emperor, am now building temples, cultivating merit, practicing charity, and ordaining monks. 'Commit no evil; perform all good. By proceeding in this manner, will I attain Buddhahood?
The masters replied, "You shall not attain Buddhahood. Any mind that involves deliberate effort is entirely within the cycle of saṃsāra.
The Great King asked, "What kind of karmic fruit will I obtain then? The masters replied, "You will obtain the reward of rebirth in the heavens. The Emperor attained [this understanding].
"Regarding the retribution of merit and longevity," the King asked, "What is the ultimate conclusion? The Master said, "When merit is exhausted, one falls. The King asked, "Where does one fall?
The Master said, "The retribution for the exhaustion of merit and longevity is fully recorded in the Buddhist scriptures. For a short while the Great King remained silent.
Then the two masters said to the King, "The mind itself is Buddha; seeing the nature is Buddha. The King asked, "What do you take to be the Way? How should one practice it?"
[The Master] proceeded. The Master said: "The sutras state: 'The entire ocean of karmic obstructions all arise from deluded thoughts.
If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true nature (dharmatā). I pray that Your Majesty will recognize this true nature, and you will naturally become a Buddha. The Great King rose.
He paid homage to the two masters and spoke of their mutual salvation from the affairs of birth and death. The Great Master said:
"For now, let me explain to the Great King the names of *tathatā* (True Suchness). First is called Buddha-nature; second, True Suchness; third, the Profound Purport;
fourth, the Realm of the Pure Dharma-body; fifth, the Spiritual Terrace; sixth, the True Soul; seventh, the Infant; eighth, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; ninth—"
It is called the School of Emptiness. Tenth is the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*). Eleventh is the Pure Consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*). These are the designations for the One Mind.

All Buddhas of the three periods of time and all twelve divisions of the scriptures are contained therein. Great King, your original nature is already fully endowed; there is no need to seek it elsewhere.
You must urgently save yourself; no one can act on your behalf. This mountain monk cannot save you, Great King. This mountain monk—
He loves and cherishes sentient beings as if they were his own infants. Encountering conditions, he immediately employs skillful means to deliver them.
If one becomes a Buddha, one must first deliver oneself. Once one has awakened to the single nature of True Suchness (tathatā), there is no need for many words.

If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have not yet realized the empty and quiescent true source, they must rely on provisional speech to establish their teachings; if they have realized the true source, they accord with the Way through wordlessness.
The Way is fundamentally without words and without speech. The Buddha said that one realizes the Way at the place where there is no effortful activity (*anābhoga*). He further said:
"Moreover, this mountain monk has been invited by Your Majesty to reside at the mountain gate; having no choice in the matter, I shall preach the Dharma for Your Majesty to repay the King’s grace."
When this mountain monk preaches the Dharma, it is like a great rain falling, universally moistening all at once according to the power of their merit.

If there are sentient beings with meager merit who do not believe in the Mahāyāna, it is like rain falling upon withered wood or scorched seeds; such are the icchantikas who lack faith. This mountain monk says:

"I pray that Your Majesty will simply contemplate the fundamental nature within yourself. If you see it clearly, everything will naturally be understood—this is the way of all Buddhas and patriarchs."

The two masters’ profound principles were all realized by him through his own direct knowledge of reality; even all provisional designations and names he likewise realized through his own direct knowledge.
Upon hearing how the two masters thus exhorted and instructed him, the Great King gave rise to great faith.

This is the Primordial True Buddha. Pervading the entire realm of empty space, there is no place among all forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects where he does not attain self-mastery.
He has no length or shortness, nor squareness or roundness; he appears according to all things and is called the Great Matter appearing in the world due to causes and conditions.
He is also called that which has no mind and yet can be named, and that which in a single thought returns to the realm of emptiness. He is without form and without appearance; this is non-existence.
It is the mind. Great King, once you have realized the mind, let the mind become like wood or stone; over time, let it forget all conditions.
Do not give rise to thoughts that measure or judge good and evil; let everything proceed as it always has. It is like a person lost on a path, or like empty space.
It is also called the non-abiding mind, the self-nature nirvana, the ineffable, and the unbound.
It is called formless; it is also called the Dharma-gate of the One Mind; it is also called Great Nirvana; it is also called Samādhi-Mindfulness Dhāraṇī;
it is also called the Ocean of the Nature of True Suchness; it is also called the Unconditioned Great Way; it is also called the Single True Dharma-Dhātu;
it is also called the Bodhisattva who neither goes nor comes; it is also called Natureless Nirvana; it is also called the Vajra [Samādhi].

It is the obscure true reality (*tattva*). It is also called the intrinsically pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*), the Tathāgatagarbha, the Prajñā of the True Mark (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*), the Buddha-nature as the primary cause (*hetu-buddhadhātu*), the One Vehicle of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad ekayāna*), the Nirvāṇa of the Pure Nature, and the True Suchness of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-tathatā*).
Furthermore, it is said: "O Great King, when first contemplating the mind, there is no mind to be contemplated; one turns toward non-existence."
Regarding the path of effort: when first contemplating the mind, thoughts arise in accordance with inversion; they arise from illusion.
Such thoughts arise from delusion, like the wind in the sky, having no place of dependence. The characteristics of such phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing;
one's own mind is inherently empty, and thus one awakens to the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). This dharma is indestructible. One contemplates the dharma of no-mind and does not abide therein.
Within the Dharma, the liberation of all Buddhas is characterized by quiescence and tranquility. One who knows this shall swiftly attain Buddhahood and extinguish immeasurable sins.
Great King, since you now know this, you are a Buddha right now. This is the wondrous gateway of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas;
it is the gateway of hundreds of thousands of samādhis, the gateway of hundreds of thousands of wisdoms, the gateway of hundreds of thousands of liberations, and all spiritual powers.

The gateway of the wondrous function of universal penetration is entirely contained within the square inch of the heart; it pervades the entire Dharma-realm and resides wholly within Your Majesty’s mind. It is inherently sovereign:
there is no triple world from which to escape, and there is no Bodhi to be realized. The Great Way is vast and empty.
Your Majesty, now that you already know your original nature, let it all go at once; do not give rise to even a hair’s breadth of further conceptualization. Thus it is understood.

One who has fully realized this sees that thoughts, perceptions, and mental constructs are beyond all deliberation. Having already known and understood this, one must not allow those who have attained knowledge to see it;
for after a long time, the fruits of the Mahāyāna will naturally manifest. This is called the "effortless effort," where effort is never in vain.
To know this Dharma-gate is also called the "thoughtless thought. This is the ancestral teacher [of the lineage] throughout all eternity, past and present.
"The profound mystery. Now, together with Your Majesty, we shall deliberate upon the secret and profound mystery before the assembly of the various sages at the gathering on Vulture Peak.
I shall explain it for Your Majesty; you have already understood it. I pray that Your Majesty will give rise to great, immeasurable, and vast vows to maintain this and proceed toward Buddhahood.
Do not undergo the cycle of saṃsāra; this is no easy matter. Thereupon, the Great King prostrated to the two masters and sighed, saying, "I am ashamed..."
I am filled with shame. Throughout hundreds and thousands of lifetimes, it is my great fortune to have encountered a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who has pointed this out to me.

Had it not been for the direct instruction of these two masters, I would not have understood this gate of emptiness, formlessness, and non-existence even after ten thousand kalpas. From now on, I vow never to betray the profound kindness of these two masters.
The two masters said to the Great King: "Simply maintain constant emptiness and stillness in every thought; in the daily use of mind, there is great cause and effect."

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* previously explained the profound ultimate meaning of the scriptures; now, however, we simply practice giving and extensively perform acts of benefit, all of which serve as gateways for assisting the Path.
We do not restrict ourselves to views of existence or non-existence; everything is free and at ease.

One should simply cultivate the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) day by day and uphold even a single four-line verse. The Master, however, asked: "Great King, what do you see before your eyes? Is there still..."

"Are there [conceptions of] self, person, sentient beings, or life-span? Great King, the Sūtra says that practicing giving for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges is not equal to upholding a four-line verse.
It is also like making offerings to the void. Great King, you must utterly awaken from delusive thoughts;

simply and suddenly awaken to right mindfulness, holding fast to it without doubt. This accumulates immeasurable and vast primary causes for the fruit of Buddhahood. This is the wondrously luminous truth."
The mind is the great awakening, perfectly pure; it swiftly leads toward the attainment of Buddhahood.
Great King, since the time of the former masters Shanshan and Shitou, this secret dharma-gate has been transmitted by me. I pray that we may meet at the assembly of the Dragon Flower.
Great King, now that you have understood the Dharma, there is no entering or exiting in its pointing-out; there is no aspect to be observed, no Buddha, and no Dharma.

Furthermore, there is not even a single form that possesses length or shortness; all things reside within me. Whether the Way exists, it is attained; whether the Way does not exist, it is also attained.

Existence is wondrous existence; non-existence is wondrous non-existence. To speak all day long is to not speak at all; this is the simultaneous negation and illumination of both, which is itself the establishing and the refuting.

This is neither establishing nor refuting; the middle way establishes that all these dharmas are universally pervasive. If one realizes this intent, then everything is both possible and impossible, and the ineffable is itself ineffable.
One knows and sees that emptiness is formless; knowing for oneself that it is formless, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is able to give rise to all emptiness.
"In one there is all; in all there is one. When the Great King heard this, he bowed in thanks and offered twenty ingots of gold to the two masters.
Neither accepted it, and they returned to the royal palace. The Great King then asked Master Xuansha, "What of this single true mind?"
Fundamentally, there is no arising or ceasing; all things are equally without going or coming. From where, then, does this present body arise? The Master said:

"It arises from the false conditions of father and mother, and immediately receives the life-force. This single thought-moment of the original consciousness-nature extends through the present and the past;

One day, while the Master was walking in the mountains with Xuansha and Zhaoqing, Xuansha said, "Look at the top of Elephant Bone Peak:
is there any Buddha-dharma there or not? If you say there is, how do you explain its existence? If you say there is not, how do you explain its non-existence?
The Master asked, "What do you say? Zhaoqing said, "It is both existent and non-existent. Xuansha said, "If it is like that, then..."
Shang asked Zhaoqing, "You understand the beginning, but you do not understand the end. The Master said, "How about this? How will you handle it?
Zhaoqing said, "Has there ever been such a thing as 'Buddha-dharma'? "How can one speak of existence or non-existence? Try saying something; is there anything at all?
Zhaoqing then asked the Master, "How would you express the phrase regarding existence and non-existence? The Master said, "It is this very thing. How would you express it?"
[The Master asked: "Existence and non-existence. Sandou said, "Zhaoqing, how do you speak of existence and non-existence?
Zhaoqing said, "What kind of mental activity is yours, Preceptor? Sandou said, "It is not this principle. The Master said, "How do you speak of existence and non-existence?
Sandou said, "Right now, it is both existent and non-existent. The Master said, "And what about you? Sandou said, "It is not an external object."
A monk came to pay his respects to the Master. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "From Lantian.
The Master said, "Why did you not enter the grass? When Changqing heard this, he remarked, "Dangerous!"
The Master gave this instruction: "To understand this matter, it is like an ancient mirror: when a barbarian comes, a barbarian appears;
when a Han person comes, a Han person appears. A monk then asked, "If a bright mirror were to suddenly come before it, what then? The Master said, "Both the barbarian and the Han person are hidden."
One day, as the Master was walking with Xuansha, he said, "On this patch of ground, one could build a seamless stupa.
Xuansha asked, "How high would it be? The Master looked up and down with his eyes. Xuansha said, "The merit and reward of humans and devas do not equal that of the Master.
As for the prophecy at Vulture Peak, you have not even dreamed of it. The Master asked, "And what about you, my son? Xuansha—
[The cloud] was six or seven feet high.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "I have already met you at the Wangzhou Pavilion; I have already met you at Wushan Ridge;
I have already met you before the Sangha Hall. (Baofu asked Geyu: "Setting aside for a moment meeting before the Sangha Hall, what about meeting at the Wangzhou Pavilion or Wushan Ridge?")
While they were meeting at Geyu, the Master hurried back to the abbot’s quarters, while Baofu entered the monks’ hall directly.
Later, as the Master and Xuansha were leaning against a fence, Xuansha asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master shook the fence. Xuansha said, "Why undergo all this hardship? The Master asked, "How about you? Xuansha said: [He remained silent.]
Furthermore, when Miedou came, there was a newly arrived monk.
The Master asked him, "What have you come for? The monk replied, "I have come to pay my respects to the Master. The Master said:
"Which one is you, Reverend? The monk replied, "I do not know. The Master stepped on him and said, "You wild fox spirit!
I grant you thirty blows.

The monk approached. The Master said, "Neither of the two paths is involved. The monk said, "How could one possibly arrive here? The Master said, "What obstacles are there?
