A monk came from Hunan. The Master asked, "How far is it from Hunan to here? The monk replied, "It is not separated by anything.
The Master held up his whisk and said, "Is it separated by this? The monk said, "If it were separated by this, you would not have arrived.
The Master, as before, struck him and drove him out. Later, whenever that monk saw anyone, he would insult the Master. A fellow practitioner of his heard of this.
I went specifically to visit him and asked, "When you arrived at Xuefeng’s place, what words were spoken? Why did you then revile him in such a manner?
He then recounted the two occasions [when he was rebuked], explaining how his fellow practitioners had scolded and reviled him. Upon hearing this, he wept bitterly.
He would regularly burn incense at midnight and, gazing toward the Snowy Peak from afar, prostrate himself in worship.
The Master asked Huileng, "The ancients said, 'Three before, three after. What is the meaning of this? Huileng then simply went out.
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "From beyond the mountain ranges. The Master said, "Did you encounter Bodhidharma?
The monk said, "It is a clear blue sky by day. The Master said, "What about yourself? The monk said, "And what else could there be? The Master then struck him.
The Master saw the monk off; after the monk had walked three or five paces, the Master called out, "Upādhyāya! The monk turned his head, and the Master said, "Be well on your way.
He then ascended the hall and, raising his whisk, said, "This one is for those of middling and inferior capacity. A monk asked, "What about when a person of the highest caliber arrives? The Master—
[The Master] raised his whisk. A monk said, "This is for those of middle and lower capacity.
The Master then struck him. The Master said, "A dead man starving by a fence of rice; a man dying of thirst at the riverbank. Xuansha said, "A dead man starving sitting inside a fence of rice;
a man dying of thirst submerged head-first in the water. Yunmen said, "The whole body is rice. The whole...
"The body is water.
[A monk] asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Why do you babble in your sleep?
When the Master was traveling on pilgrimage, he visited the Venerable Wushi Guan. As soon as he knocked on the door, Wushi asked, "Who is it? The Master replied, "The phoenix."
The boy said, "What are you coming for? The Master said, "I have come to devour Old Guan. Baizhang then opened the door, grabbed him, and said, "Speak! Speak!
As the Master hesitated, Baizhang pushed him away and shut the door. Later, after the Master had established his own community, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"If I had been able to enter Old Guan’s gate at that time, where would you lot—this bunch of wine-dregs eaters—have gone to search for me?"
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The entire earth is this gate of liberation. Yet, though one holds out a hand to pull others toward it, they refuse to enter.
At that time, a monk stepped forward and said, "I cannot blame you for being angry with me, Master. Another monk said, "What is the use of entering? The Master then struck him.
The Master was presented by the King of Min with ten oranges and ten tangerines each, which he sent via a messenger.

The King sent a note asking, "Since they are of the same color, why are their names different? The Master returned them with the seals intact. The King then dispatched another messenger to ask Xuan Sha about it.
Shanshan covered a sheet of paper with his hand.
As he ascended the hall and the assembly had settled, the Master rolled out a wooden ball. Xuansha then seized it and placed it back in its original position.
On another day, because Xuansha had come, the Master rolled out three balls at once. Xuansha immediately assumed a prostrate posture. The Master said:
[The Master] asked, "How many do you usually use? The monk replied, "Three is one; one is three.
Because a monk then asked, "I beg the Master for instruction on the most essential point," the Master said, "What is it? At these words, the monk attained great enlightenment.
When the Master saw Elder Nanji off, Nanji performed a woman’s bow; the Master folded his hands and responded, "Yes, yes."
The Master struck his forehead with his hand and then returned home.

As he was about to pass away, he himself composed an inscription for his stupa along with a preface, saying: "That which exists by virtue of conditions undergoes formation and decay from beginning to end.
That which is not obtained through conditions remains eternally firm throughout kalpas. To be firm is to abide; to be subject to decay is to be abandoned. Although..."

Yet, as the time for our parting has not yet arrived, what prevents me from making preparations in advance? Therefore, I have layered stones to construct a chamber, trimmed wood to form a coffin, and moved earth and gathered clods to create a niche;
all matters are now complete. With my head toward the south and my feet toward the north, I lie here across the mountain.
I only pray that when the time comes, those who share my path will not oppose my intent, and those who know my heart will not alter my resolve. I entrust this to you most deeply, once again.

Exhortation. I trust you will exert yourselves. Even if in another day the heterodox were to propagate [the teachings], how could they compare to the present time when the true eye is propagated through the esoteric?
Reflect well upon this; reflect deeply upon this. The inscription says: "The brothers form a cross" (Xuedou’s commentary says: "A country has no two sovereigns," and also says: "Do you know?").
With one heart, they wear a single rite (*fēngxíng cǎoyǎn*; also: "Directly give"). The local lord is called Songshan (*sìgù fěijué*; also: "Look"). The Egg-Stupa is named Nandī (*dúlù xiāngyǐ*;
also: "Precipitous"). Furthermore, there is the Hu Family Tune (*yīxī yīdōng*; also: "Great Difficulty"). You all must know this for certain (*zìnán zìběi*; also: "Understood").
I sing the bellowing of the earthen ox (*wén mò jǔtóu*; also: "Ha ha"). You respond with the neighing of the wooden horse (*jiàn yīng*).

Close your eyes. It is also said: (Clapping hands). Just look at the fifth and sixth months—(how could it be in vain? It is also said: "In harmony"). Slices of ice fill the long streets—(the matter is no triviality; it is also said: "In accord").

[The suffering of] the fire being extinguished when the fuel is spent—who would it accompany after [death]? He also said: "Live well. In his secret chamber, he became as rotten as mud; [one must reach such a state]. He also said: "Exert yourself.

In the third month of the Wuchen year of the Kaiping era, he manifested illness. The military governor of Min ordered a physician to attend him, but the Master said, "I am not ill," and ultimately refused to take medicine.
He left behind a verse to entrust the Dharma. On the second day of the fifth month, he went to Lantian in the morning and returned home in the evening to wash his body. At midnight...
He entered nirvana at the age of eighty-seven and with fifty-nine years of ordination seniority. A stupa was erected for him in the abbot’s quarters of this very monastery.
The Master’s verse says:
"The passage of time is fleeting, a mere moment; how can one dwell long in this floating world? At thirty, I crossed the mountain pass."
2. It has been over forty days since I entered Min; though others have not failed to examine me repeatedly, what has already passed must still be gradually eliminated.
To report this to the court of the purple and crimson ranks: the Lord of Yama fears not those who wear the golden fish badge.

Wandering through the cypress forests and green mountains, there is neither preference nor aversion. On all four sides there is no path from which one comes; dwelling in a place where none have reached, one’s emergence is ultimately beyond measure.
This was said because a student asked a question.
The affairs of others are ended by others; one’s own affairs are settled by oneself. All phenomena are encompassed within a single kṣaṇa—what need is there for further coming and going?

Sòng Chéngzhǎo suddenly announced his departure to return to his hometown. He has traveled a long and arduous path through the snow-capped mountains for three autumns; yet Chéngzhǎo possesses not a single thing.
Reading the poems of Han Shan, one finds them pitiable:
this man of Han Shan speaks much and talks even more. He builds fences and barriers across the road; how can he compare to one who seeks the radiance directly?
On Fish Drums, Two Poems I have temporarily become a fish drum;
my suspended head suffers for the sake of the assembly. When the master-monks drink tea and eat rice, they take up the mallet and strike my belly.
Though my body is covered in scales and shells, there is not a single thing within my heart. While the cormorant looks across the stream, I vow never to enter the lake.
Pitiful little fish-drum, born of heaven and nurtured by the earth. Unable to digest even a morsel of gruel or rice, it makes a sound from an empty belly.
It startles the monks’ sleep at every moment; for the indolent, its vexations grow long. The abbot’s quarters become a scene of clamor and noise; it would be better to beat a wandering drum instead.
Tending the oxen at early dawn, they graze upon the dewy grass; until midday, they are well-satiated. Once the oxen are full, they have no further thought of eating;
with nothing else to do, the young oxen sing their cow-song.
I urge people not to say it is easy to go; to truly go is also very difficult. Though empty space fills the world, the deluded sit in restlessness.
If you have a sincere, compassionate heart, I urge you not to engage in empty talk. Should you suddenly meet a person of clear vision, they will laugh themselves to death upon encountering you.
A withered tree conceals a dragon; greedy for sleep, one does not hear the bell. When dawn breaks and one rises early, one suddenly realizes what kind of dragon this is.
Looking down, one does not see the earth; looking up, one does not see the sky. If you wish to know the whereabouts of the white ox, simply look before the skull.
Bodhidharma’s journey was from afar; do not fail him. Examine and contemplate with meticulous care; it would be well if you were to suddenly awaken.
Every person possesses the eyes of heaven and earth; do not look askance through deluded sentiments. The lands of the Ganges River are all swallowed up;
once swallowed, what is there to say? What is there to say?
A dragon hides within a withered tree; when the thunder rolls, it must be startled. Those who are startled are few; those who are not startled are many.
The summit is as white as snow; all waters share one deep source. The site of practice is level as the palm of a hand; the mind of my school transcends that of the Buddhas.
A fishing line cast upon the Yangtze River; the roaming fish take up the silk line. The hook’s bait is heavy with grace, yet it lightly mocks the song of the Patriarchs.
Feet planted on the ridges of Xiangji, head resting on the slopes of Maming, the body lies within the white clouds—its divine radiance hidden across ten thousand miles.
If you can grasp my final phrase, you and I shall be of one branch.
The winter melon is long and clumsy; the gourd is pointed and round. Its brilliance fills all under heaven; look at its blackness, vast and boundless.
Have you not seen the ornamental pillars by the roadside? The world is in a frantic bustle, all of one kind.

The plectrum of the lute turns with the hand, yet the wondrous melodies of Guangling remain unplayed. Were there someone who could play them, a single performance would exhaust all the melodies under heaven.
In this world there is one thing; I urge students to take it up. Though one may lack even half a coin for livelihood, one can pass down wealth through kalpas.
To ascend to heaven one does not borrow a ladder; to traverse the earth there is no path. This is the place that encompasses all of heaven and earth—O sons of Chan, awaken to it with urgency!

At the dawn of the tiger-hour you refuse to rise; you greedily linger until the dimming light of the late afternoon. Like a fish caught in a net, you are plundered until your belly swells and bursts for the hunter.
With the heavens full of clouds, the path is not seen; lost for ten thousand miles, you vanish into oblivion. I ask you, O person of the world: when will you attain Buddhahood?
Grinding a tile will not produce a mirror; yet the void will always have its moon. Act with urgency and grasp it for yourself; do not allow yourself to be reduced to fragments over many lifetimes.
Thrown high, it does not reach the heavens; cast low, how could it settle upon the earth? When the sun’s orb has hidden behind the mountains, you turn your head only to search for your own nose.
I now exhort you on the Path: cease your preoccupation with written words. I also urge the wood-gatherers: exert yourselves and do not deceive one another.
Having lived many lifetimes without leaving the household life, you have suffered toil for ten thousand kalpas. Today, renounce your attachments; take your vow and look back no more.
Spring frost fills the heavens with cold; I observe your blackness spreading vast and wide. The white ox is ever before the skull—urge you to examine it closely.
I inform you all for your knowledge: the true nature does not lie on the path; the physical body merely requires rest. Why toil so bitterly?
One must know that it is not obtained from another; why laboriously seek it day and night? One’s own pearl is utterly transcendent beyond the three realms;
it is neither a sage nor a sensory object.
The sky is clear and bright, the green ridges divide; ten thousand li of empty space are utterly free of a single speck of cloud. What a pity that people of this age do not awaken!
Those who are willing shall travel together through this Dharma-gate.
Ten thousand *li* without a blade of grass; far-reaching and solitary, severed from mist and clouds. Throughout kalpas it has always been thus—what need is there to leave the household life?
As for the robe of the Utpalaka once promised to Lady Zeng in years past, even until now the shuttle has not moved. For today, let us simply follow the clouds and waters.
Go! Who can wait for a duck to become a goose?
To the Venerable Master Shi:
"Excellent, O Wayfarer! Having suddenly stilled the great potential, you stand majestic and profound. By what means shall this be revealed? At the summit of a thousand mountains."
Ten thousand layers of green robes, embraced by wind and clouds; I have never known this floating illusion, wandering in feigned folly wherever I go.
As the severe frost approaches, my hair hangs down to my eyebrows; I cannot distinguish monk from layman, leaving all conjectures to doubt. May this subtle merit awaken me.
The rain falls and the clouds fly.

It is not yet the time for one who has not received the precepts to leave the household life at twenty; leaving the household life at twenty is precisely the proper time. Now that you have encountered the conditions for the official ordination platform, [do not let this opportunity pass].
Agreed. I am but a clumsy, old novice monk.
Reflecting on my own thoughts before I reached Xuefeng, I was fond of grasping at the ephemeral world with casual doubts; yet when it came to the Dharma-gate, it was not the Dharma.
The Dharma, in its ultimate essence, has neither self nor teacher.
The Master himself inscribed a wooden plaque, saying:
"When the deluded body approaches a mirror to reflect its image, the image and the deluded body are no different. If one wishes to remove the image while retaining the body, one does not know how."
The shadow-form is eternally empty; the shadow-form has never been different from its source. One cannot grasp it as either existent or non-existent.
If you harbor aversion toward the mundane and attachment to the sacred, you will forever float within the sea of birth and death.
If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata. There is one who secretly saves others;
alas, how can people know it? (Great kindness is difficult to repay.)
The Master was practicing zazen at Kumo-an (the Withered Tree Hermitage). While he was drying wheat in front of a water mill, he personally inscribed this verse:
"Before the hermitage, throughout the day, there are no wolf cubs; At the base of the mill, all year long, there are no sparrows."
To this day, there have been no wolves or tigers in the mountains. Furthermore, when grain was spread out to dry before the mill, not even a single bird would alight;
everything occurred exactly as the Master had predicted.
The Master inscribed the following on the beam in front of the Sangha Hall:
"Today does not guarantee tomorrow; one must always prepare for a thousand years ahead.
This was the regulation established by Master Zhijue Yan-shou of Yongming Temple, who set up this stone inscription.

Now, as for those who have left the household life, they first model themselves upon the prescribed rules and solemnize their conduct. Once their practice is refined, one may say that such a person is fit to seek out an enlightened teacher.
Next, one must discern the underlying principle; for the True Path is profound and still, transcending all time from antiquity to the present without meeting with opposition.
It encompasses the myriad categories of the ten directions, yet has never been dual from its inception. Such matters are explained by recourse to worldly conventions.

If one acts as an abbot by relying on the semblance-dharma (xiangfa) to establish a dwelling, gathering the hearts of all beings to live together, desiring that the hundred rivers return to a single source and all streams reach the great ocean—as it has been said of old: "A household has no two masters; a kingdom has no two kings.
Two masters will surely contend; two kings will compete. How much more so for the monastic community, which must be free from contention? Where there is contention, there is no Sangha.
The aim is to ensure that throughout the three periods of time, the ten thousand establishments are maintained, the minds of the people are at peace, and their continuity is never lost.
Should there be those who seek refuge in monasteries and request to change from white robes to black, they shall all be required to submit to a single presiding authority.
If there are no two masters, disputes will be avoided. Simply by following the regulations established by our late master Fuyong, one will understand their meaning.

As for the two monasteries of Lantian and Zhangji, they shall merely take turns each year to appoint a monk who has completed his term of service to manage them, providing support from beginning to end.

Regarding the stupa courtyard: the permanent endowments for the maintenance of this courtyard shall be used for the monks and others residing therein; by no means may the abbot be selected through private deliberation.
Should there be among the assembly those who are elderly or infirm and unable to provide for their own needs, a capable novice (śrāmaṇera) shall be appointed to attend to them from beginning to end.
If no novice is available, a śrāmaṇera shall be appointed in turn; if no śrāmaṇera is available, a fully ordained monk (bhikṣu) shall be assigned by rotation.
From beginning to end, one must attend to them with care, never failing in this duty.

If there are lay donors from villages or towns who, with sincere devotion, invite [the community] to chant the Buddha’s name at a ritual site (dōjō), it is essential that the assembly deliberate and appoint only those capable of performing the Dharma rites;
this shall avoid vulgar criticism and suspicion.

Sāmaneras, novices, and fully ordained monks (mahābhikṣus) of this monastery who leave the community without cause, failing to take leave of the administrative officers and the assembly, shall be expelled upon their return.
If they return for minor reasons and without grave transgressions, they shall be penalized by performing one hundred prostrations and then permitted to remain.
However, if at that time they do not comply with these instructions and agreements, [they shall be expelled].
One must also leave the monastery.

If the resident monks or other officials of the monastery should arbitrarily inflict corporal punishment with wooden staves, it will cause people to feel uneasy; therefore, one should leave the monastery during the daytime.

Regarding the above-mentioned articles concerning the affairs of the abbot’s office, it is hereby commanded that the administrators, the chief officers, and the monastic community alike shall collectively observe and uphold them, without transgression.
Let them be maintained from end to beginning. On the tenth day of the intercalary sixth month in the fourth year of the Guanghua era, the śramaṇa Yixun issued this notification.
The Master left these final instructions for all people: "All things arise from the conditions of foam-like illusions; their coming and going are uncertain.
For over forty years, I have never failed to admonish you with bitter words. Lately, the Buddha-dharma has grown thin, while people are diligent only in worldly affairs. As for..."
Regarding offerings made out of faith to teachers and preceptors: once they have passed away at the end of a hundred years, there is no further way to repay their kindness through virtuous deeds.

Since worldly rites are no longer appropriate, it is likewise fitting that we exercise some measure of discernment. When my four elements disperse, I have already prepared a wooden coffin and a stone niche in accordance with my long-held wishes;
these shall be arranged as planned. No separate tomb or pagoda shall be constructed, nor shall a spirit altar be established.
One must not wear mourning garments. Some may even wear a piece of cloth one chi long and shed a single drop of tears; such persons are not śramaṇas and are not my followers.
How much more so for those who wail to the blue heavens—this is merely a vulgar custom that greatly dishonors our school. There are some, however, who do not comply with this.

Expel [those who violate] according to the Dharma. Within this monastery, those of seniority shall follow and respect the wisdom of their predecessors, and all shall mutually honor and transmit these teachings;
you must not recklessly act in opposition. Hereafter, the abbots shall all follow the regulations established by our late master Fuyong.

Furthermore, since we have never personally ordained a female disciple (bhikṣuṇī), after my passing, you must by no means allow them to enter the monastery gates, so as to avoid worldly censure and reproach. For...
Regarding the permanent regulations: from this point forward, including the Upper Hall, one must by no means hold separate discussions regarding the abbot.
On the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Kaiping era (the Wuchen year), this was promulgated by the Śramaṇa Yicun.
The regulations established by our former masters for the governance of the monastery were proclaimed and issued as official mandates, to be implemented according to their original terms:
it was forbidden to privately ordain novices, to hold private landholdings, to arbitrarily maintain cooking pots and pans, or to consume food separately from the community;

furthermore, matters such as entrusting assets to the monastic estate, mortgaging or leasing temple buildings and estates, and engaging in commercial speculation were strictly prohibited in accordance with these rules. This was during the third year of the Qiande era, in the year of [the cyclical sign].
Established on the twelfth day of the fifth month of the year Yi-chou by Qian Chu, the Great Marshal of the Armies of the World and Acting Minister,
King of Wuyue.
The end of Volume II of the Recorded Sayings of the Great Master Zhenjue of Xuefeng.
Lao Zhenjue emerged as a towering figure during the fragmentation of the Five Dynasties.

Since the moment he attained liberation from the very bottom of the bucket after Deshan’s single blow, he reached a state where the moon was cold over the Turtle Shop and the snow had cleared from Elephant Peak. He took the essence of *amṛta* in a single ladle and manifested great function through three balls.
His lineage split into two schools, and his Way transcended all preceding patriarchs. It was as if he were thundering a hundred billion peals of lightning.
For hundreds of generations beneath the Four Heavenly Kings, its fame has grown ever more magnificent.

When it comes to the turning of the pivot of wisdom and the display of instruction—the sublime words of the Great Teaching—they flow forth from his breast, covering both heaven and earth. Like a single performance on the Guangling Terrace, they cause the minor strings to feel ashamed and fall silent, never to sound again.
Having recently passed through the calamity of the conflagration, the woodblocks and records have not been preserved. The layman Jueru of Fucheng has raised funds to re-carve them.

Thus, I have propagated this widely. Should readers be able to lend an ear beyond the surface of mere reputation, they will know that the "Yangchun" and "Xuequ" melodies, as well as the sublime and correct tones of the Great Odes, are all contained herein.
If you still do not understand, beat the drum and invite everyone to look!
In the summer of the year Xinyou of the Zhizhi era, the monk Wuyi, a successor to the Patriarchs at Xuefeng,
respectfully appended this postscript to the Chronological Biography of the Great Master Zhenjue of Xuefeng:
the second year of the Changqing era of Emperor Muzong of the Tang dynasty, the year Renyin.
The Master was a native of Nanan County, Quanzhou. His surname was Zeng, and his father’s name was Mian. It was in this year that the Master was born.
His family had served the Buddha for generations; their ancestral cemetery was located on Mount Yangmei, forty-five li to the west of the city.
Ichō Hōshō prostrated himself before him; this is what the common people call "the foreign monk’s prostration.
The third year, *kaimō*; the fourth year, *gōchin*;
the first year of Emperor Kōjō’s *Hōryaku* era, *gyoshi*.

In the second year, the Bingwu year, when the Master was five years old, he developed a strong aversion to pungent foods and raw vegetables. Even while in his swaddling clothes, he would be moved to tears upon hearing the sounds of bells and Buddhist chants, or seeing banners, flowers, and sacred images;
whenever he performed a prostration, his countenance would visibly change, causing all who saw him to marvel at him.
The first year of Tahe of Emperor Wenzong, Dingwei;
the second year, Wushen; the third year, Jiyou;
the fourth year, Gengxu.
When the Master was nine years old, he earnestly petitioned his parents to leave the household life. Because they cherished him deeply, they did not grant his request.
[The years were] the fifth year, Xinhai; the sixth year, Renzi;
and the seventh year, Guichou.
When the Master was twelve years old, he accompanied his father to visit Yujian Temple in Putian.
There he saw Vinaya Master Qingxuan and immediately prostrated himself, saying, "This is my teacher. He then remained there to serve him.
The eighth year, Jiayin; the ninth year, Yimao;
the first year of Kaicheng, Bingchen; the second year, Dingyi;
the third year, Wumu.
The Master was seventeen years old when he shaved his head and subsequently changed his dharma name to Yicun.
The fourth year, Jiwu (4719); the fifth year, Gengshen (4720);
the first year of Emperor Wuzong’s Huichang era, Xinyou (841); the second year, Renxu (842).
The third year was Guihai; the fourth year, Jiazi;
the fifth year, Yichou.
The Master was twenty-four years old. In this year, an imperial decree was issued to purge the Buddhist teachings. The Master, dressed in Confucian attire, went to visit [Master] Fu.
Chan Master Hongzhao Lingxun of Mount Furong in the province was taken under the wing of [Master] Zhao, who regarded him as a vessel of great potential and kept him by his side.
In the sixth year, the year of Bingyin,
when the Master was twenty-five years old, Emperor Wuzong passed away, and the edict proscribing Buddhism was relaxed.
In the first year of the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong, the year Dingmao, the Master was twenty-six years old.
In this year, he received an imperial edict to return to Buddhism and again took Hongzhao as his master.
In the second year, Wuchen,
and the third year, Jisi,
when the Master was twenty-eight years old, he went to Baocha Temple in Youzhou to receive the full precepts.
In the fourth year, Gengwu,
and the fifth year, Xinwei,
when the Master was thirty years of age, on the ninth day of the fifth month of that year, Venerable Hongzhao entered parinirvāṇa.

In the sixth year, *wenshen* (Ren-shen), and the seventh year, *guiyou* (Gui-you), when the Master was thirty-two years old, he took leave of the Zeng family to travel as a wandering monk (*yufang*). He spoke a verse which said: "In years past, I once vowed to [become] an Upādhyāya..."
"Luó! Even until this very day, he has not yet moved his shuttle. For now, let us follow the clouds and waters;
who can wait for a duck to become a goose? Thereupon, he joined Yantou Huo in the assembly of Daci Huánzhong and became friends with Huánzhong’s chief disciple, Qīnshān Wénsuì.
He traveled south to Jiangnan, where he ascended Mount Tóuzi three times and visited Mount Dòngshān nine times.
The Master once served as the head cook at Dongshan. One day, while he was washing rice, Dongshan asked, "Which do you remove first:
the sand or the rice? The Master replied, "Sand and rice are removed all at once. Dongshan said, "Then what will the assembly eat?
The Master thereupon turned the basin upside down. Dongshan remarked, "Your karmic affinity does not lie here," and so the Master went to study under Deshan.
In the eighth year, Jiashu (854),
and the ninth year, Yihai (855),
when the Master was thirty-four years old, one day Dongshan asked him, "What have you been doing? The Master replied, "I have been hewing a trough."
Shanshan said, "How many blows of the axe did it take to form this? The Master said, "It was formed by a single blow of the axe.
Shanshan said, "That is still a matter of 'this side. What about a matter of 'that side'? The Master said, "It reaches the point where there is nowhere to apply the hand.
Shanshan said, "That is still a matter of 'this side. What about a matter of 'that side'? The Master then ceased speaking.
The tenth year, Bingzi; the eleventh year, Dingchou;
the twelfth year, Wuyin; the thirteenth year, Jimao;
and the first year of the Xiantong era of Emperor Yizong, Gengchen.

In the second year, the *xin-si* (xinhai) year, when the Master was forty years old, he went to visit Deshan. The Master asked Deshan, "Regarding the matter of the ancestral vehicle (*zongcheng*), does a student still have a share in it or not?
Deshan struck him with a staff and said, "Speak! At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
It was like the bottom falling out of a bucket.
This was in the third year, Renwu,
and the fourth year, Guiwei.
When the Master was forty-two years old, he served as the head cook at Deshan. One day, because the meal was late, Deshan personally carried his alms bowl down from the Dharma Hall.
Seeing this while he was drying his towel for wiping the bowl, the Master said, "This old fellow! The bell has not yet rung and the drum has not yet sounded;
where are you going with your bowl? Deshan then returned directly to his quarters. The Master recounted this incident to Yantou.
Tou said, "The Great Master Deshan does not understand the final word.
When Deshan heard this, he had his attendant summon Yantou to the abbot’s quarters and asked, "Do you not approve of this old fellow? Yantou secretly conveyed his meaning, whereupon Deshan desisted.
The following day, when Deshan ascended the hall, it was indeed different from his usual manner. Yantou went before the Sangha Hall and patted [the wall].
Zhang laughed heartily and said, "I am glad that the old master of the hall has understood the final word;
on another day, no one in the world will be able to withstand him. Nevertheless, he shall live for only three years."
In the fifth year, Jiashen, and the sixth year, Yiyou, the Master was forty-four years old.
He and Yantou took their leave of Deshan together. The Master had previously traveled with Yantou.
Upon arriving at Aoshan Town in Lizhou, they were detained by snow. As Yantou woke from his sleep, he saw the Master sitting upright and scolded him, saying, "Brother Cunen!
Brother Cunen! Why do you not go back to sleep? You look just like a local deity in a village of three households.
The Master pointed to his chest and said, "I am not yet settled here. Yantou said, "According to your realization, [is it] point by point..."
Tonglai came forward. The Master cited the recorded exchanges between Yanguan, Dongshan, and Deshan, all of which Yantou had dismissed.
Thereupon, Tonglai attained great enlightenment beneath those words. Rising up, he called out to the Master, "Today is finally when Aoshan achieves the Way."
In the seventh year, the Bingxu year, when the Master was forty-five years old, he set out with Yantou and Qingshan wishing to visit Linji.
While on the road, they encountered the Senior Monk Ding, who said, "Master Linji passed away on the tenth day of the fourth month. The Master said, "I..."
Jiā was of meager merit and did not see the Upādhyāya; I do not know what words were exchanged.

It is certain that the "True Person of No Rank" (wùwèi zhēnrén) dialogue was raised. From that point on, the three parted ways: Yántóu went to Lóngshān, Qīnshān stayed at Lǐyáng, and the Master returned to Fúmián.
Later, while traveling through Jiān'ān, he built a hermitage there to dwell in, which is now known as Huánglóng and Shuāngshí. The two... [monasteries].
This is that temple.
The eighth year was Dinghai,
and the ninth year was Wuzi.
At the age of forty-seven, the Master, reminiscing about the site where he had studied at Fuyong, returned to reside in the Stone Chamber—this being Lingdongyan.
In that same year, Weishan and Lan’an arrived leading their disciples.

The Provincial Governor of Shanglian, Li Jing, sent a letter requesting the Master to establish a monastery at Mount Yi, the place where the Real Man Wang had ascended to heaven west of the city. This is the present [site].
This is Xichan Temple.

In the tenth year, the Jichou year, when the Master was forty-eight years old, he sat in meditative seclusion within a stone chamber. Among his disciples, there were those who urged him to emerge into the world [to teach], but the Master remained deeply [resolute].
He declined. At that time, his senior fellow student, Master Xingshi, remarked, "Your virtue and Way are most eminent;
nothing less than the excellence of Vulture Peak or Monkey River is sufficient to welcome you. They proposed using Elephant Bone Peak as your title, and the Master accepted it.

In the eleventh year, the Gengyin year, the Master was forty-nine years old. Toward the end of spring that year, Master Shi Bo considered Xianggufeng to be a strategic stronghold and visited various elders to seek the divination for the site of a monastery.
At that time, there were the lay devotees Fang Xun, Xie Xiao, and Chen [Xing] from the eastern side of the mountain.
The attendants vied with one another to observe the precepts and vowed to offer the Jeta Grove. Subsequently, Hongyuan also offered half of Chenyang as a material offering for the Dharma.
Thereupon, a hermitage was established to the north of the Liangying Terrace in Chenyang, and the Master was invited to reside there. Once he had arrived,
Sitting there, he was filled with joy and said to Shishi: "I have labored to select this place; I shall dwell here.
That winter, the Master, together with Shishi and his elder brother, ascended the summit of the peak to survey the scenic features. Upon returning, they deliberated on the name of the mountain.
Some said that woodcutters had found elephant bones at the peak; others said that the mountain top is covered in accumulated snow throughout all four seasons. Thus, it came to be known by two names.
When they spoke of this together, the Master smiled and said, "It shall be so. Three hundred paces above, he found a superior site.

Previously, Master Shi had purchased the foundation for a hermitage from Master Fang; Master Fang then donated the mountain forest. Later, Masters Xie and Chen followed suit, joyfully making their offerings.
From that time on, offerings from the *dānapāramitā* converged like spokes in a wheel. Some donated wealth, while others established agricultural estates, which gradually expanded.

In the twelfth year, the *xinmao* year, when the Master was fifty years of age, he extensively renovated the temple buildings. Even wooden figures contributed their labor, hastening the completion of the work. The assembly...
He took this as a cause for joy.
The thirteenth year was Renchen;
the fourteenth year was Guisi.
The Master was fifty-two years old. Amidst the remainder of his labor in timber and earth for construction, he sang and chanted according to the occasion, never once slackening.
When disciples arrived, there was no room to accommodate them.
In the first year of the Qiánfú era of Emperor Xi (the Jiǎwǔ year), the Master was fifty-three years of age.

At that time, Huang Chao was in rebellion on the eastern mountains; the Master lamented the precariousness of the state’s destiny and the suffering of the common people, who were submerged in the fires of war.
In the second year, the year of Yiwei (635), when the Master was fifty-four years old, Governor Wei donated three hundred strings of cash for the construction expenses.
From the year of Gengyin (630) until this time, a total of six years had passed, by which time the temple was fully completed. The monk Zhi-lang then departed for Chang’an.

The matter of the upper hall was decided by drawing lots. At that time, it happened to be the Day of Responding to Heaven (Yingtian Jie). Consequently, [the Emperor] bestowed upon him the Xuefeng Temple of Yingtian.
In the third year, Bingshen, when the Master was fifty-five years old, he sent a letter to Yantou, saying: "This letter from me, your senior brother..."
After attaining the Way atop Mount Ao, he has remained until this very day, never hungry despite eating his fill.
In the fourth year, the *dingyou* year, when the Master was fifty-six years old, while traveling outside the monastery, he reached Chenyang and said: "I have arrived here for the first time."
The mountain attained three realms; this was the third. It could serve as the site for the construction of a stupa; the current foundation of the stupa is this very place.
The fifth year, Wuxu.
The Master was fifty-seven years old. At that time, the Nestled Bandits (Chao-kou) entered Min from Zhejiang. In this year, the practitioner Leng Dao came to pay his respects.
Leng was a native of Yanguan.
It was the sixth year, Jihai.
In the first year of the Guangming era, the gengzi year,
when the Master was fifty-nine years old, the rebels from Chao entered Xiang.
In the first year of the Zhonghe era, the xinchou year—
When the Master was sixty years old, his assembly numbered over fifteen hundred people. Whenever anyone came to visit him, he would immediately roll out three wooden balls:
one would be left in his quarters, and two would be hidden inside the stupa. That year, Beidou appeared in the world and resided at Puying Temple in Meixichang; later, he moved to Xuansha.
In the second year, the Renyin year, when the Master was sixty-one years of age, Li Jing, the Military Governor of Lianzhou, donated one hundred thousand strings of cash;
Chen Gong, the Minister of Works of Yingchuan, donated three hundred strings of cash; and Wei Gong Chubin, the Regional Inspector, donated two hundred thousand strings of cash.
The funds were deposited at Taiping Wangban Village. The retired official, Lord Li of Longxi, donated one hundred and thirty-eight strings of cash.
Subsequently, he established the Damu Monastery (Dàmù Xiàsì) west of the city. In that same year, an inner court official returning from Min Province spoke of the Master’s virtue and conduct;
[the Emperor] received this with great reverence.
By the imperial decree of Emperor Xizong, an edict was issued to the relevant authorities of Fuzhou to compile a record of the Master’s spiritual conduct.

At that time, the local scholar Chen Yanjiao submitted a memorial detailing his actual virtues for presentation to the throne. Consequently, the Master was granted the honorary title of Great Master Zhijue (True Awakening) along with a purple robe and *kāṣāya*.
In the third year, Gui Mao, and the fourth year, Jia Chen, the Master was sixty-three years old.
At that time, Li Kuyong defeated Huang Chao at Taishan Hukou; when the Master heard of this, he...
Xi. First year of Guangqi, Year Yisi; Second year, Year Bingwu;
Third year, Year Dingwei.
The Master was sixty-six years old. On the eighth day of the fourth month, Yantou encountered bandits; he let out a great cry that was heard for many tens of li before his life ended.
His body was cremated, and countless śarīra relics were produced. When the Master heard of this, he was filled with profound sorrow.
In the first year of Wende (Wushen), the first year of Emperor Zhaozong’s Longji era (Jiyou), the Master was sixty-eight years old.
He established the foundation and constructed a stupa at Chenyang; this is what was previously referred to as the "Third Realm."
The pagoda was completed on the seventh day of the seventh month of that year. The Master himself composed the inscription for the pagoda. At that time, his senior master Xingshi passed away;
the Master wept for him with great sorrow and raised him for burial on the eastern slope of West Mountain. The Master wrote the record for the pagoda as follows:

The body has departed from the conditioned world; the stupa returns to the seamless state. For a thousand autumns, the pines shall guard the mountain; for ten thousand years, the cranes shall frequent the ridge. The Master’s Dharma name was Haeng-sik;
his secular surname was Gao, and he was a native of Yongjia. He received his formal training at Fuyong Mountain. From the year of Jichu (1099).
When he first established this mountain, Xing was truly enlightened regarding geomancy; he broke new ground by founding the mountain gate and opening the waterway.
From its origins to its conclusion, his merit was no small matter. On the fourteenth day of the eighth month of that year, he passed away at the old monastery.
He was sixty-seven years of age and twenty-six years in the monastic order.
The first year of Dàshùn was Gēngxū,
and the second year was Shēnxī.
At the age of seventy, the Master traveled once more through Wu and Yue. He first arrived at Yongquan on Mount Tiantai.

In the first year of the Jingfu era, the Renzi year, when the Master was seventy-one years old, he stayed at Lingyin during the summer of that year. Later, he went to Guoqing Temple and subsequently arrived at [Mount Tiantai].
He traveled by boat along the Yangtze River and subsequently visited Yuyang Monastery; on each occasion, there were dialogues and karmic encounters [between him and the masters].
This was in the second year, Gui-chou (the first year of the Qian-ning era), and the following year, Jia-yin.
At the age of seventy-three, the Master returned to Min and stayed at the site of the Zhenyang Pagoda.

The Provincial Minister, Lord Langgong, invited him to reside within the provincial government offices to expound upon the profound essentials of the Way. He immediately provided the funds to construct a Dharma Hall at the pagoda pavilion.
That year, the temple was moved to Chenyang; this is the current monastery. Through a bond of karmic affinity, he had at that time a dharma-heir disciple who succeeded him.
There were fifty-six individuals who propagated the Great Dharma, including Xuansha Bei, Ehu Fu, Yandong Xiu,
Zhaoqing Ling, Yunmen Wenyan, and Gushan Yan.

In the second year, the Year of Yimao (835), when the Master was seventy-four years old, he led his assembly on a southern tour. At that time, Huang Niepan had foreknowledge of the Master’s arrival and went out to meet him with a staff in hand.
Upon reaching Suxi, they encountered one another by chance. The Master then asked, "Where have you recently departed from? Niepan replied:
[Daowu] said, "Pizhi Rock. The Master asked, "Is there still a master within the rock? Bian struck the Master’s sedan chair with his bamboo staff.
The Master then came out to meet him. Bian said, "Wanfú (Ten Thousand Blessings) to Elder Lang. The Master immediately performed a formal prostration of a man.
Bian performed a prostration of a woman. The Master asked, "Are you not a woman? Bian then performed two more prostrations and [resumed] using his bamboo staff.
He drew lines on the ground and circumambulated the Master’s litter three times to the right. The Master said, "I am a person within the triple world; you, Master, are one outside the triple world.
You should go on ahead; I shall follow later. Baopan then returned first. The Master subsequently arrived and stayed at Nangshan for several days.
Baopan attended to him and provided for his followers without anything being lacking. Next, they went to Waguan.
At that time, Wang Yanbin, the Grand Tutor of Quanzhou, established the Dongmili and Zishou monasteries and invited the Master to reside there, paying him great honor and respect.
Meanwhile, Wang Shenzhi, the ruler of Min, who held the position of de facto sovereign, was deeply impressed by the Master’s spiritual transformation.
He once led a congregation of a thousand followers at the East and West Pavilions to preach the Dharma for the King.

Initially, he donated three hundred thousand coins to construct twenty bays of annexed buildings; subsequently, he donated another three hundred thousand coins to build the Dharma Hall, the circumambulatory corridor, the abbot’s quarters, and other structures.
In the third year, Bingchen,
and the fourth year, Dingyi,
Chan Master Sheng of Zhaozhou entered nirvana.
In the first year of the Guanghua era, the year Wuma (758),
when the Master was seventy-seven years old, the King of Min invited him and Xuansha to enter the inner palace to discuss the Buddha-mind seal.
Upon hearing such instructions from the two masters, the Great King gave rise to great faith and immediately established a great vow with a sincere heart.
He received and upheld [the teachings], never once wavering in his resolve. The Great King again invited the two masters into the inner palace to discourse on the Buddha-dharma.
He rearranged the incense tables and strictly forbade any leakage of the proceedings. Furthermore, he ordered three of the Inner Secretaries to record the Dharma words from behind a screen.
The Master then requested the Buddhas, nāgas, and devas to bear witness as he transmitted the Buddha’s Mind-Seal to the King. He then donated money.
Four hundred thousand *ding* were used to construct over a thousand large halls and buildings, all of which were magnificently completed.

When the Master first arrived at this mountain many years ago, a lay devotee from the south of the mountain named Lan Wenqing, recognizing the Master’s spiritual transformation, established a hermitage beside the ancient *cing* tree by East Pond in his own residence and invited the Master to take up residence there; that tree is now withered.
This was Mudan. Lan Gong further established a vihāra at Chengyang Village and invited the Master to reside there;
this is the site of the old monastery today. Seeing that the assembly had grown large, Lan Gong converted his own residence into a major monastic center and moved the Master to preside over it.
He subsequently received a formal petition from the Ruler of Min, Zhongyi Wang.
Emperor Xizong bestowed the title of *dānapati* (檀越主) upon Lan Wenqing, appointing him as the Regional Commander (節度使) of Weiwu.
The eldest son of the Protector King Minghu was Yingchao, the Divine Lord Tongyou; his younger brother, the monk Shouyuan, was the Venerable Compassionate One.
They now serve as the local deities (*shêtiandi*) of this mountain. Later, Wenqing, along with Yang Danniang, their second son Yingchen, and others, moved [to another location].
He established his residence at Maoyang Village to fulfill his aspirations, and further donated twenty villages of farmland and gardens;
these are the present-day Lan-tian, Tai-ping, Da-mu, and other villages.
In the second year, Jiwu (1079),
when the Master was seventy-eight years old, the King of Min dispatched an envoy bearing a silver folding chair to present to him.
In the third year, Gengshen (1080).
The Master was seventy-nine years old. By imperial decree, his temple was renamed Yingtian Guangfu Temple.

In the first year of the Tianfu era (the Xin-you year), when the Master was eighty years old, on the tenth day of the intercalary sixth month of that year, the Master was about to submit a formal petition regarding the abbotship and—
The regulations for monastic conduct are established to instruct the assembly of disciples. In general, regardless of whether a matter is great or small, all affairs are entrusted to the abbot.

Just as the hundred rivers flow into the sea and all streams originate from the same source, and as there can be no second king in a nation nor a second master in a household, so it is with the Sangha who dwell in non-contention;

where there is contention, there is no Sangha. When the mind is at peace and relations are harmonious, the continuity of the tradition is maintained. This applies even to matters concerning monasteries, estates, and pagoda temples.

All matters have established regulations. The elderly and the infirm shall be provided with care and support as required by principle. Those capable of chanting Buddhist scriptures may do so to respond to external circumstances.
Should the monks commit any transgressions, they shall be punished according to the gravity of the offense.

Since they are not administrative officers, it is not permitted for them to wield the staff arbitrarily, as this would cause unrest among the community. For all affairs, simply follow the regulations established by our late master, Master Fuyong. Thus, [it is concluded].
To know its meaning.
The second year was Renxu,
and the third year was Guihai.
The Master was eighty-two years old. The community of monks at the temple grew daily, yet the annual income was insufficient. The buildings were gradually leaking, and he wished to carry out repairs;
however, the scale of the project was vast, and there were no monks such as Wuliang or Wuyue who would resolve their minds to solicit the necessary resources from the public.
The circular halls and ornate pavilions remained as they were, in accordance with the Master’s practice.
