The substance is firm. I wish to grasp my new poems to inscribe upon past events, yet I regret that I lack a sharp brush as large as a carriage beam.

At the Ten-Thousand-Pine Pass, who planted these ten thousand pine trees all in a row? Two lines of them flank the path leading into the monastery. From half the sky, the clear whistling of the wind lasts through the autumn.
The cool shade covers the ground so completely that one might lose one's way in broad daylight. Amber vapors float upward to form emerald mists;
golden flower petals fall, blending with the fragrant mud. I shall gather this vast, azure hue, dwelling amidst the drifting clouds like a crane in its nest.
The snowy peaks stretch far and wide, their ridges reaching out through the falling snow. Where the pure white blossoms gather, the path of coming and going remains open.

High as jade steps ascending the celestial palace, steep like a silver bridge leading to the lunar realm, the immortals walk with empty chants as their bodies shimmer; the traveler climbs the perilous heights as his shadow lingers.
In the dim light, I seek out the plum blossoms, ascending straight to the mountain peak. Looking down at the plains, all are one uniform color.
Longmian’s Fangshan resembles a dragon’s slumber, stretching diagonally across the landscape; this body is ever shrouded by white clouds. After the rain has passed, scales emerge from my skin.
A. The trees are so dense that no one can see its claws and fangs; when will this transformation encounter a thunderbolt? It slithers through long days, exhaling mist and clouds;
one knows not in what era it was finally subdued. Having traversed heaven and earth, how many years and autumns have passed?

At the Mañjuśrī Terrace, mists and clouds stretch for ten thousand acres like a pile of brocade. This was once the terrace where Mañjuśrī manifested his transformations. A fine breeze from the Western Extreme passes over the South Sea;
the Dharma rain from the Central Heavens descends below. The lion with its variegated brush has mounted the clouds and departed; the Dragon King wears his golden girdle.
The moon returns. Where can one find the numinous traces of a thousand ages? Wildflowers bloom by the side of the Cool and Refreshing Stone.
The Ancient Mirror Stand is like jade, without flaw—the Ancient Mirror Stand. Before heaven and earth were yet divided, it opened of its own accord. A whole sky of rain washes away the dust.

Pure. As the clouds withdraw from ten thousand ravines, the moon’s reflection arrives; within the golden and azure paintings, the morning casket opens. Amidst the halo of the icy hare, verdant moss grows long;
how might it fly upward beyond the azure heavens, dispersing divine light across the nine realms?
The Golden Turtle Bridge:
A golden turtle emerges from the earth, about to soar into the void; it spans the long stream amidst azure mists. Its reflection does not follow the flowing water away;
its illusory form must surely be like that of the Sleeping Dragon. One is startled to think the Milky Way connects here with the magpies, yet again one marvels as the clear waves reveal [the bridge].
A rainbow. Do not seek Mount Penglai within the vast blue seas; travelers forever rely upon it to cross from west to east.
On Luohan Cliff, divine monks dwell in lofty seclusion atop Mount Tiantai. I ask: when will they cross the sea to arrive? The ancient path through the clouds leads to Fangguang Temple.

The temple stands where stone cliffs border the Terrace of the Brahma King; its numinous light at midnight joins with the bright moon. Sacred traces from a thousand years past rest upon the green moss;
this extraordinary landscape remains eternally youthful and never grows old. Even today, one may still see the hundred flowers in full bloom.
Tiyun Ridge:
This ancient ridge soars loftily toward the azure sky; its ten-thousand-fathom celestial ladder spans a flying rainbow. When the clouds part, the bird-path reveals layer upon layer of peril;
as one enters the pine-gate, the way is open at every step. The divine retinue often wanders within the verdant trees, while the songs of woodsmen drift afar across the emerald expanse.
Amidst the mist, how many times have I myself repaired the clogs of Mount Dongshan? Ascending and descending before and after, I have whistled in the evening breeze.

At Elephant Bone Peak, the Great Elephant has always possessed a majestic and powerful presence. Who was it that carved its skeletal frame out of mid-air? Its marrow having been exhausted, it has transformed into a lattice of empty space.
The rock’s exquisite emergence is yet another feat of the Creator’s power. One suspects it is a colossal body submerged in an ancient ravine, with no long trunk to stir in the spring breeze.
When shall a primal energy arise in a single night, so that it may once again carry a divine monk across to the lands of the Rising Sun?
The incense-stone is exquisite; upon its fine surface, incense is well-ground. Heaven and Earth have concentrated its essence by the ancient path. Its pure fragrance does not dissipate with the wind;
its brilliance and essence linger long amidst the mist. Vaguely, it resembles chicken-tongue incense floating in the warmth of spring; in a daze, it is like dragon’s spittle.
The night is cool. Who could it be that has left behind these traces of human touch? As one passes by, who would not inhale the lingering fragrance?

At the pond for releasing living beings, the autumn air is refreshing and the spring air is harmonious. Upon this pond for releasing life, many creatures are set free; they fly and leap at will, unconfined.

Bound, yet following every departure and arrival, one is freed from the snare. Within the canopy of lotus leaves, the transformative rain is held aloft; in the mirror of water-lily flowers, the waves ripple with benevolence.
Looking down upon the clear and shallow waters, one beholds the reflection of heaven; ten thousand forms flourish in harmony, together vibrating and rubbing against one another.
The Dip-Moon Pond is limpid; this level pool spans several *mu*. A single ripple does not stir, and the night light is cold. The Goddess who plays with pearls ascends into the void;
Lady Cháng’ér gazes at her reflection as she stands before the mirror. White and azure have long been blended throughout antiquity and today; the blue heavens reflect above and below.
Gathering in harmony, the crystal palace is free of even the slightest obscuration; at times, dragons and serpents are seen coiled at the bottom of the sea.
At Wangzhou Pavilion, the evening sun sinks in the west while the waters flow east. Ascending alone to the high pavilion, I gaze toward Zhaozhou; clouds rise in the azure sky, veiling the cranes.
Shadow. Rain ceases on the Penglai isles, revealing the head of the Tortoise; those who once tasted the tea have gone—who knows where?
Only the flowers remain in the Jetavana grove, passing through several autumns. Having leaned against all twelve balustrades to chant, a single bright moon remains upon the azure isles.
The Chozik Spring lies before the emerald cliffs at the foot of Xuefeng Peak. Where the monk’s staff was planted, a stream of spring water was opened;

its sweet flavor far surpasses that of stone marrow, and its flowing fragrance must surely carry the scent of dragon’s spittle. Cool and verdant, moss seals the traces of the sacred site; its purity blends with the rustling sounds of pines and bamboos.
The Night Lute: The stream turns and its mechanism is profound, yet it cannot be retained; in the end, it returns to the great ocean and drenches the azure heavens.

Responding to the tide, the spring in the emerald pool is a numinous spring that responds to the sea tides; as the tide comes, the spring flows forth, and as it departs, it recedes. One inhalation and one exhalation reach through to the heavens.
The earth shifts between shallow and full with the passing of day and night; below, water spirits dwell in the vast, murky depths, while above, pure vapors rise to counteract the stifling heat.
Fearing to disturb the slumber of the dragons in their deep lairs, I dare not venture to play the jade flute.
In the first year of the Tiānshùn era, the year of Dīngchū, the śramaṇa Yuántán,
Right Street Jueyì of the Sēnglùsī and seventy-sixth generation abbot of Xuefēng who succeeded his patriarch,
respectfully composed verses following the original rhyme for the twenty-four scenic views.
On Mount Xuefeng, six flowers congeal into white lotuses; beyond the mountain ridges, drifting clouds shift from pale to deep. As summer enters the "Fu" period, a slight heat is felt;
as the season shifts to mid-autumn, it is already like winter. Silver mounds fall in scattered layers across a thousand steep peaks; jade steps jut out in jagged rows of a hundred.
A hundred-foot pine tree; how many times have I gazed from atop the Rain-Falling Terrace? Its light flickers through the pavilions as the frost-bell tolls.

Beside the Terrace of Jewels and the Terrace of Jasper lies the Pavilion of Variegated Flowers; towering upon clouds and mists, it sends its green hues afar. Many-feathered birds perch within the Multi-Jeweled [Pavilion].

Pearl flowers are arranged in golden vases upon the trees; incense smoke from agalloch drifts before the screens like waterfowl. Purple bamboo branches strike the bells at the corners of the pavilion.
Leaning against the jade balustrade, he waves the *vīraja-cīvara*; half in the sky, yellow cranes carry the immortal spirits away.

The Lan-tian Estate is orderly, with Lan-tian fields surrounding the Snow Peak. The recluse plants jade, and the jade abounds. Along the path, plum blossoms fall, their fragrance difficult to disperse;

from crevices in the crags, springs fly forth, the water naturally pounding like a mortar. Mountain maidens pierce through the clouds idly gathering azure greens; mountain monks, amidst the rain, gaze upon the scene.
The plowman’s field; where vermilion peaks and azure waters lie, smoke-wreathed villages stretch afar. Nine miles of pines deepen into emerald layers upon layers.
Within the ancient wood of Kumu Monastery, the interior is as vast as a palace. An old monk sits here, discoursing on emptiness; his roots coil through the earth’s axis, reaching the blue seas.

The sea’s reflection falls upon the bamboo blinds, shining through the embroidered lattice. At the edge of the clouds, the stone bamboo (shizhu) sways with evening green; after the snow has fallen, the mountain tea (shancha) reveals its spring red.
Facing this, there is no need to inquire about matters of prosperity and decay; all are contained within the profound realm of illusory transformation.

The three balls, the hall, the bed, the lion throne, the fly-whisk—how wondrous and boundless! His fame has spread across the lands of China and the barbarians for five hundred years. The three kicked balls are not fixed vessels;
a single sphere of true qi merges with the celestial circle. The even numbers circulate from the original odd number; coming and going among humanity in an instant.
Ascending to Heaven. Among the thousands and hundreds of people, who could have understood? Xuan Sha gave a subtle smile as he stood before the hall.

One Dongshan—whose fame is transmitted throughout the world as the foremost mountain. Within the mountain there is a cave, extraordinary compared to the human realm; its jade-like fungi and precious herbs are in full bloom.
Outside, amidst the drifting mists and auspicious clouds, I happened to see golden lotuses springing from the earth; in an instant, I beheld white cranes returning from the heavens.
Liu and Juan of Tiantai should be held in laughter; having left their cave longing for the immortals, their hair has already turned gray.

A lofty pavilion on the mountain slope is erected amidst the azure clouds. Its painted rafters and carved beams face a jade-paved balustrade. Its imposing presence commands the mountains and rivers with natural grandeur;
It preserves the purity of wind and moon, needing no further expansion. Across the stream, crimson reflections flow with the fading light; Within the hall, verdant shade brings its cool retreat.
The morning chill. How laughable is this gathering at Lan-zhu on Mount Gui; we linger freely by the winding waters as cups flow.

At Huacheng Pavilion, leaning on my staff, I ascend the high terrace at leisure. Before my eyes, mists and clouds gather like a pile of brocade. Green bamboos sway in the breeze beneath the bright moon.

Shattered. After the rain falls on the green mountains, the white clouds part. The Prince of the Dharma dwells within the city manifesting his transformations; the Son of the Buddha comes from beyond many kalpas.
Is this not the place of the Teacher’s skillful means? Celestial flowers and the rain of Dharma linger together.
A single stele without characters lies by the side of a path; ancient dragon-script and bird-seal inscriptions were once carved upon it. The moon slants and the plum shadows grow faint like ink;

the rain washes the mossy traces until they are as slippery as saliva. Heaven, loving its wondrous text, would have seized it with thunder and lightning; Earth, restraining this strange stone, has covered it with snow.
The frost is firm; it is required that the stars shine night after night. For many years no one has constructed even a single rafter.

At Wansong Pass, ten thousand trees of lofty pines thrust toward the Milky Way. Their solitary statures stand out in elegance, arranged like *bodhi* trees. Their shadows are faint in the moonlight, their roots rooted in the frost.
Cold. After the rain, the shadows thicken as the grassy paths grow obscure. When yellow pollen drifts, fragrance wafts through the valleys;
where white fungi grow, the vapors steam the mud. Before the pass, *lang-zhan* bamboo is planted at intervals, attracting azure pheasants and purple phoenixes to settle there.
Xuěqiáo has long dwelt amidst the silver mountains and iron walls; a lofty, solitary path is rarely traversed by men. The celestial deities sow jade to pave the crystalline steps;

the feathered immortals ride the clouds to tread upon the Buddhist halls. Entering the Nine Heavens in a dream, the soul becomes vast and remote; upon awakening, the moon shines over a thousand realms.
Hazy and dim. Peaks turn and ridges wind deep within the clouds; far removed from the paths of the red dust.

Where the dragon slumbers, the terrain is just beginning to undulate, the mountain’s form half-tilting and askew. It is as if the dragon’s slumber were veiled by mist; beneath the pines, withered roots coil and twist in ancient age.

Bones. Beside the bamboo, fresh shoots burst forth like spiritual fangs. At dusk returning to the ancient temple, one hears the True Dharma; at dawn heading toward Donglin, one chews upon the crimson mists.
Deep in the night, the moon rises over the vast blue sea; a single pearl from its jaws radiates brilliant light.

At the peak of Mount Six-Petaled, the Mañjuśrī Terrace is a mass of emerald green; the Terrace of Mañjuśrī seems to approach the Flower Terrace (Tuṣita). Vimalakīrti lies upon his sickbed displaying illness;
the Dragon Girl presents her pearl as it rises from the sea. Fragrant mists swirl around the lion throne; the Elephant Peak is bright and pure in its scenery.
As the stars turn their cycles, those who understand will grasp the meaning of cool clarity. When spring returns to the great earth, the flowers bloom of themselves.
The ancient mirror-stand was originally a bright mirror; it is not a stand at all. If the mirror is clear, the mind opens of itself. Deep and secluded, the green phoenix gathers its reflection.

There is nothing; the graceful jade hare sends forth its light. Within it, the color of the sun is contained like scattered sparks of fire; on its back, the verdigris of copper peels away like speckled moss.
When clouds have dispersed across the edges of the earth and the ends of the heavens, the Zen mind shines with brilliant clarity upon the myriad worlds.

From afar, the Golden Tortoise Bridge reveals Mount Ao soaring into the azure void; the Ao Bridge again spans the midst of the celestial ford. The thoroughfare leads to the capital through a thousand paths;
the waters flow from their source as ten thousand streams in one accord. By day, there is no trace of the staff that ascends to transform; in the blue heavens, its shadow connects with the divine.
Flying Rainbow: When will the eminent monk who went west return? By the bridge, the pine branches seem to lean toward the east.

At Luohan Cliff, a single staff flew and came to rest upon the High Terrace. From the heights of the precipitous cliff, no human reaches; by the streamside, the rain washes away the dragon-subduing traces.
The alms bowl; by the cliff’s edge, the wind rises from the Tiger-Dwelling Terrace. A solitary black bear cradles its cub while peering into the green trees;
a white deer leads its fawn, licking the azure moss. Knowing well that all outflows have been utterly forgotten, the iron staff knocks at the gate, yet none open it.

The Cloud-Ladder Ridge stretches far and wide, its stone steps suspended in the clear sky. As the mountains turn, they cast a horizontal arc like a rainbow drinking from the mountain stream. Broken geese seem to fall from the heavens;
returning crows flash as they connect with the sun’s edge. From afar, human figures appear faintly on the horizon; up close, the lute-like music of the pines fades into the distance.
Amidst the mists, one knows not in the still night that the bright moon has risen; the tinkling of celestial girdles stirs the fragrant breeze.
Elephant Bone Peak stands firm—how majestic and powerful that great beast! The land of Yì has come to take refuge within the Buddha-field. Once, he was granted the *Bhadracari-praṇidhāna*.
Through his efforts, he continued to practice asceticism under Master Xue; how could these solitary bones remain forever buried in stone? How could the two tusks ever again emerge from the wind?
Though his illusory body has been consumed by fire, his name remains; the true spirit has always resided to the east of the ocean’s edge.

The fragrant grinding stone brings down the star-like essence of the lunar spirit. Who would say it grinds away beside the azure heights? In clear weather, its smoke-filaments part not from the wind’s caress;
at night, its refined blossoms bloom, carried aloft by the moon. It does not compare to the liquid essence of purple-wool tea; it is fit to be paired with camphor rain.
Moderately cool within. Now, in these mountain hermitages, the passing light extends afar; why need one always be perfumed by the fragrance of liberation?

In the Great Sage’s realm of longevity, the harmony of Heaven warms all; the various classes of living beings released there are many indeed. How laughable that one would attempt to dig a pit upon a level path!

A pitfall! Yet I sigh for those who spread their silken nets upon level ground. In vain do they claim this place to be a sea of benevolence; it only serves to cleanse the hearts of men and wash away the waves of true desire.
Cast aside the three-sided net of the merchant class, and let the vital energy of heaven and earth be harmonized together.

Who carved this moon-dipping pond? A square pool, as wide as a mirror. Its clear waves are profound and still; the moon’s radiance is cold. The wild horses of the world swirl in confusion within the void;
the brilliant jade wheel is viewed upon the water. The cassia washes its fragrance, floating rich and fragrant; the pine hangs its slender shadow, reflecting back.
Lank-lank. This old monk has not used Rǔgāng’s axe; he leaves behind this gnarled and sprawling root.

The Peak of Wàngzhōu stands tall, with its waters flowing through a thousand mountains and ten thousand ravines. Looking toward one another, in what state does Old Zhào dwell? His mind races across the vast void where heaven ends.

The place where my vision ends at the vast, azure horizon where the waters reach their limit. Rain washes the Ao Peak within the realm of my verse; clouds obscure the crane’s path as I gaze toward the mid-autumn sky.
If one wishes to inquire about the divine mechanism, for what reason does it exist? Know that it resides on the Ninth Continent of Penglai and Yingzhou.

Carrying my staff, I seek its source before the Elephant Bone Spring. In an instant, as I plant my staff, sweet water wells up. Its clarity makes one suspect it is the *hanghai* nectar flowing through hidden channels;

its fragrance makes one marvel that a divine dragon is secretly spitting forth saliva. Splashing against the rocks, it surges and tosses with "crab-eye" bubbles; emerging from the stream, it resounds with a mournful, sobbing cry.
The strings of the *kūn* lute; a single pool of stillness, a mirror of luminous clarity. My Zen mind shares in its vast expanse under heaven.

Responding to the tide, it gushes forth from among the springs and rocks, harmonizing with the surging waves. Its breath waxes and wanes along with Yin and Yang. Drawing from it, many people are filled to capacity.

Shallow. Rising and sinking follow their own seasons as one gauges the morning sky; I have long used pure flavors to nourish my poetic lips. Yet I laugh at those who crave fame and spread their clamor through the world.
I hide my clumsiness, lying high upon the Snow Mountains; when the moon is bright, I wash my ears and hear the flute at night.
General Poem on the Twenty-four Scenic Views: The Jewel Site of Xuefeng is near Lantian;
Three Dry Trees and a Single Cavern-Dwelling. A Transformation City halfway up the ridge and the Unnamed Stone;
Ten Thousand Pines and Snowy Peaks where Longmian dwells. Mañjuśrī’s Ancient Mirror beside the Golden Turtle; The Arhats Ascending the Clouds upon the Elephant.
Gudian; Xiangshi; the Liberation Pond that reflects the moon; Wangzhou; the Chao-chuan Spring where the staff was planted.

Written with nine prostrations by the bhikṣu Zhiming, a distant descendant of the mountain-dwelling lineage of the present age, to the Great Master Zhenjue, who descended in response to his wheel of vows, tore asunder the net of craving, and emerged from the dust of the world, his wisdom and understanding surpassing all others.

His quest for the Way was sincere and earnest; he sought out friends and masters. As long as he had not yet attained realization of the essential meaning, he did not consider whether mountain valleys were steep or level, nor the distance of the journey, near or far.
He braved hardships and treks two or three times over, never succumbing to indolence midway. Once he had received the seal of certification from Master Deqiao, [he remained steadfast].
Still feeling that his aspirations were not yet fully realized, he received the encouragement and guidance of Yantou; only then did he first utter the words regarding attaining the Way at Mount Ao.
Upon returning, he founded this monastery, where the unbidden assembly was so vast there was no room for them. Those who ascended the hall and entered the inner chamber numbered forty-five.
Yunmen and Xuansha were the foremost among them. The dialogues and exchanges used to test the spiritual capacity of their disciples are recorded in volumes;

however, these have been damaged by insects and consumed by fire, with their preservation and destruction occurring more than once. Fortunately, there were those who rescued what had fallen and repaired what was in decay, yet even they have now passed away as before.
Master Ming Xingan, while residing on the mountain, lamented that the Way does not reside in language or written words. It is not...

If one merely speaks of words and letters, the Way will not be revealed. Having been unworthily entrusted with this weighty charge, how could I bear to sit idly by while the ancestral Way is forever neglected and never propagated?

Fearing that future students would lose their vision, I searched far and wide until I discovered a collection of lost manuscripts in the Chuangyue Tower at Mount Dao. I personally oversaw the transcription and commissioned artisans to carve them into printing blocks.

Now that the work is nearly complete, I have drafted this preface to inform those who come after. (Note: The character "忝" [tiǎn] is used here to express a sense of being unworthy of the honor; the missing character following it is likely "職" [zhí], forming the term "忝職" [tiǎn zhí], meaning "to be unworthy of one's office. The phrase "永弛而弗張" [yǒng chǐ ér fú zhāng] means "permanently slackened and not spread.")

I have recorded this for my own sake. At a time when my duties were so numerous and demanding, he was able to take pity on the scattered loss of his ancestors' witty sayings, restoring what had been broken or missing.
His resolve is truly commendable; I have thus written a brief account of these matters and appended it to the end of this scroll.

Dated the first month of winter, after the full moon, in the Jiachen year of the Chenghua era of the Great Ming, by the Chief Administrator (Dugang) of the Buddhist Monastic Administration (Senggangsi) of Fuzhou Prefecture.
Zhìmíng, the eighty-fifth abbot of Gǔshān Chán Monastery, burns incense and records these reflections with prostrations:

Alas! We live in the age of the final dharma, when the True Teaching is fading away. We have grown ever more distant from the authentic teachings of the Sages, while the heterodox paths of fierce Māras and outsiders blaze forth.

What a pity that my birth was so late; I did not encounter the era of a Buddha. Consequently, the pure resonance of the Dharma is beyond hearing, and its wondrous interpretations are difficult to penetrate.
Am I not, indeed, free from shame regarding my life thus far? Nevertheless, fortunate as I am to possess past causes (*pūrvahetu*), I have had the honor of joining the ranks of the black-robed.

Although I have searched through the Buddhist scriptures (*vaṃśaka*) and fished for knowledge within the Tripiṭaka, gazing upon that mountain of wisdom towering high and beholding this ocean of meaning profound and deep, I have rejoiced to have swum its waters for several years, gradually dispelling my ignorance and delusion.
Truly, it may be known that I am practicing "daily increase and daily decrease" (*zhì rì yì rì suǒ*). Even if I have not yet reached the threshold [of ultimate realization],...
Aha! Having already constructed the gates and walls, one gazes upon the excellence of this magnificent mansion; surely there must be a way for me to ascend it.

Who would be willing to let their time pass in vain, content to remain ignorant and dull-witted, and thus abandon learning? What is called "within a single scroll, the sky of one's nature shines brightly" is indeed not false.
Thus, before the Great Master Zhizhen had fully penetrated his Zen mind, he did not shrink from...
Yunshui also once endured the hardships of three ascents and nine descents. Later, he attained realization at Mount Ao;

his mind and eyes opened wide and clear, and he directly realized the stage beyond doubt. Only then did he fulfill the aspirations of his life. Eventually, as he sat upon the majestic peak, his thunderous voice shook the world.
Manifesting the full majesty of a lion, he poured forth the nectar of the *tīrtha* and received those of the highest capacity.

Regarding their spiritual capacities, he employs manifold methods of guidance to draw forth and uplift future generations, providing benefit and support for those yet to come. From within the state where there is nothing to be said, he speaks;

from within that which has never been heard, he reveals what is heard. His compassionate heart is most earnest—what is it not to say that one who was once a wanderer feels particular pity for the traveler, and one accustomed to fondling his guests is ever mindful of the one who fears intoxication?
He desires to cause everyone’s defilements to vanish and their awakening to become pure, universally enabling them to...
Each and every one reaches the fundamental reality and forgets the emotions; suddenly they realize the divine pearl is held in their own grasp.

They do not seek it elsewhere; the supreme treasure is within their bosom. They ought to rejoice in this themselves. Thus, the principle is expressed through written characters, yet the truth transcends the realm of speech.

As the ancients said: "To understand speech does not depend on the tongue; to be able to observe does not borrow from the eyes. Therefore, the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter, like being born blind.
A tortoise encountering wood is like a fine mote meeting a needle. Śākyamuni, in a former life, sacrificed his entire body to repay the price of half a verse;
the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita sold his heart and liver to seek the Prajñāpāramitā. How could one dare to disregard the words of the Sage?

(I, [Name], once perused the recorded sayings of the Patriarch and cherished them as precious treasures. Because those who borrowed them were stingy and failed to return them, I subsequently encountered a setback.)
The official tablets were consumed by fire and reduced to ashes; I sighed with deep regret, fearing that his illustrious reputation might be stifled and fail to be transmitted.

Concerned that future generations would have no standard for reflection, I immediately sought out and borrowed the texts to publish the complete edition, desiring that for a thousand years hence, the spirit of my ancestor’s heart may shine forth and remain ever-present.

Now, comparing the sequencing of these two versions together, there are occasional minor discrepancies in the phrasing.

Regarding the shifting of preceding and succeeding sections: although there is no mutual increase or decrease in their underlying principles or facts, it is like the *Lunyu* (Analects), which exists in both the Qi and Lu recensions.
While the *Lunyu* of Lu alone circulates today, one must nevertheless be familiar with the arrangement of the Qi recension.
What has been published this time is the "Lu edition" of Xuefeng, while that which is appended is the arrangement of the "Qi edition. Furthermore...

Written on a spring day in the Renwu year of the Genroku era (1702) by the old monk Manzan.
